title: Two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems for high-dimensional data: noncentral normal-reference inference
summary: We study noncentral normal-reference inference for high-dimensional two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems. Within the Gaussian reference, a shifted null law is accurate if and only if covariance-weighted signal energy is negligible relative to the trace of the squared covariance. We establish the sharp uniform fourth-root error order over unrestricted spectra and a linear bound under spectral spread. A separate spectral-range criterion determines when signal magnitude alone suffices. An augmented spherical reference gives finite-sample calibration for Gaussian samples and asymptotically recovers Gaussian-reference local power under projection fourth-moment bounds and control of diagonal fluctuations, without a dimension-to-sample-size restriction. For unknown Gaussian covariance, explicit trace and hollow-Gram confidence bounds turn the linear approximation bound into a simultaneous, computable certificate over local effect ranges. Eigenspace signal energies describe directional power, while a two-point argument limits estimation of unknown local power. Simulations with 10,000 evaluation replications per configuration examine unequal and noncommuting covariances, severe sample imbalance, non-Gaussian observations and the informativeness of the certificate.

title: The exact region of the Average Rectangular Volume and Spearman's rho, with an application to arachnitude
summary: The average rectangular volume ($\ARV$) of a bivariate aggregation function is the average of its volumes over all axis-parallel rectangles of the unit square; for a copula, it is the expected copula volume of the rectangle spanned by two independent uniform points. We determine the exact region of the pairs $(\ARV(C),ρ(C))$, where $C$ ranges over all bivariate copulas and $ρ$ is Spearman's rho. The region is compact, convex and symmetric, and its upper boundary consists of three analytically parametrized arcs. A previously proposed family of shuffles of Min generates one arc, but only on part of its range; the other two arcs are generated by singular copulas whose supports contain hyperbolic branches. The boundary is continuously differentiable away from its left endpoint $\ARV=\frac{11}{120}$, where it has a vertical tangent. The proof uses a folding transformation and explicit Kantorovich potentials for a family of optimal transport problems. Finally, we show that the arachnitude, a rank correlation used in actuarial practice, is an affine transformation of $\ARV$, so that the result also describes the joint region of Spearman's rho and arachnitude.

title: Fundamental Limits of Honest Inference with Heterogeneous Transfer Sources
summary: Transfer learning can improve precision by borrowing information from external sources, but how much improvement is possible while maintaining valid inference? We address this by studying honest confidence intervals for a target parameter using multiple sources with heterogeneous prespecified discrepancy bounds. Under local information and admissibility conditions, we establish a universal lower bound on interval length for procedures maintaining uniform coverage. A scalar information equation characterizes the bound, revealing how precision depends jointly on source sample sizes and discrepancies. Large source samples need not yield greater precision gains when their discrepancies are large. When discrepancies are unrestricted, honest intervals cannot improve upon the target-only rate, even when all sources are unbiased. For the Gaussian location model, we calculate optimal source weights and construct honest intervals attaining the lower bound order, establishing sharpness. We extend the lower bound theory to semiparametric models through parametric submodels. For the Cox proportional hazards model, we verify the information conditions under which the lower bound applies, including under right censoring.

title: Discrete total variation under the multinomial, Part 5: cyclic total variation
summary: We study the cyclic discrete total variation obtained by adding the wrap-around edge to the usual open-chain statistic. Under the uniform multinomial law the cyclic symmetry recombines the same per-edge, adjacent, and disjoint covariance blocks used for the linear statistic, but with different multiplicities, and this simplifies the variance: the bin-independent leading coefficient \(2A+4B\) carries over, the constant-order correction collapses \emph{exactly} to \(β_c(n)=β_1 n\) (no \(n^0\) or \(1/n\) tail; obtained directly here, and already reached in Part~2 through the transfer identity), and a conditional second-order coefficient \(γ_c(n)\) is given. The exact finite-\(N\) cyclic--linear transfer identity of Part~2, read order by order, both delivers these and, as its main consequence for the \emph{linear} statistic, explains the traveling mode of the linear variance: comparison with the (first-order) mode-free symmetric cyclic profile shows that deleting one edge introduces a rising contribution whose balance against the falling cyclic bulk creates a ridge at \(n\asymp\sqrt{K_0N}\) with local optimizer \(K_0=C_1/β_1\). Uniform control of three ridge blocks proves this optimizer on every compact ridge window, upgrading the previously heuristic \(\sqrt N\) mode law to a theorem; the global localization of the exact maximizer remains open. We also record the corresponding cyclic reference-centered statistic under a fixed alternative and the leading Nabeya variance formula for the matched non-uniform cyclic statistic. Throughout, ``exact'' refers to the asymptotic coefficient in \(N\); the operative symmetry is cyclic stationarity (rotation invariance), not exchangeability.

title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
comment: 67 pages, 7 figures. Lean 4 formalization and code: [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23768172](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23768172)
summary: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = ρ/ (μ_i + ρ)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $Δ_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $Ψ(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $ω^* = (4ν^2 Σ/ c')^{1/3}$, $c' = σ^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(ρ)$, and the plug-in strength $ρ^* = σ^2 / (nδ^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $ρ_{\mathrm{eff}} = ρ(e^{ζq} - 1) / (ζq)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.

title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

title: Exact power spectra and effective dimensionality in critical block-GOE networks
summary: Criticality in neural networks is crucial for optimal information processing. Recent studies have shifted focus from static criticality to frequency-dependent behavior, particularly in oscillatory systems modeled by block-Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (block-GOE) matrices. However, analytical tools to predict spectral properties such as power spectrum and effective dimensionality remain scarce. In this work, we derive exact solutions for the network-averaged power spectrum $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{S}(ω)]$, the network autocovariance $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{C}(τ)]$, and the normalized effective dimensionality $D_N(ω)$ in block-GOE ensembles. These results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how oscillatory networks operate near criticality, offering insights into the dynamic balance between stability and flexibility in large-scale neural systems.

title: Null-Corrected Conditional Coverage in Materials Property Prediction: A Five-Dataset Replication
comment: N pages, 15 tables. Extends and partly revises arXiv:2608.07589. Submitted to Data-Centric Engineering. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22213087
summary: Uncertainty quantification for materials property prediction increasingly reports conditional coverage, coverage within strata of the predicted value, alongside marginal coverage. The worst-bin statistics used for this are downward-biased in finite samples, a known defect that applied materials work does not generally correct for. We replicate a single-dataset conditional coverage study across five regression datasets (n = 437 to 21,263), seven interval methods and 50 random splits each, correcting the worst-bin statistic against its expected value under exact conditional validity. The null is simulated from realized per-bin test counts and referenced to each method's own marginal coverage, separating marginal miscalibration from uneven coverage. On the smallest dataset the correction runs from 0.061 to 0.096, between a third and two thirds of the shortfalls actually reported, against 0.009 to 0.011 on the two largest. Split conformal prediction's failure survives the correction on four of five datasets; two conclusions of the antecedent study do not. Conformalized quantile regression, characterized there as a negative case, fails on one dataset only. Cross-fitted normalized conformal prediction, grouped there with the successful methods, fails on three of five. Group-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction stays below our significance criterion on every dataset, yet exceeds the null on three of five under an octile refinement of the variable it calibrates on. A level-matched ablation locates that uniformity in group-conditional calibration rather than in the elevated quantile level, and removes Mondrian's apparent width cost entirely. Conditional coverage evaluations should report the null distribution of the worst-bin statistic used, the method's realized marginal coverage, and the resolution of the evaluation partition relative to any partition the method calibrates on.

title: Geometry-Aware Smoothing Selection for Noisy Scattered Surface Reconstruction: Evidence from Synthetic Benchmarks and Water Quality Data
summary: Sampling geometry may influence both reconstruction stability and the smoothing needed to control noise. This study distinguishes geometry-dependent failure of exact multiquadric radial basis function (RBF) interpolation from variation in validation-selected smoothing. A synthetic benchmark crossed four response families, four 16-point geometries, three slice levels, five observation regimes, and 24 repeated holdouts, yielding 17,280 method-level evaluations. Clough--Tocher cubic interpolation, exact RBF, and smoothed RBF were compared, followed by a Water Quality Portal pilot with 1,950 complete activities. On the synthetic shared-valid domain, exact RBF achieved the lowest noise-free mean RMSE (0.0206), whereas smoothed RBF performed best under noise (0.1807 versus 0.2414 for cubic and 0.6106 for exact RBF). Clustered-gap support produced the largest noisy exact-RBF RMSE (1.2706). Geometry added little explanatory power for log-transformed smoothing: the combined model had $R^2=0.4259$, compared with 0.4096 for noise alone. Reported failure-regression results suggest a stronger geometry signal, but remain unverified without their original model specification. In the environmental pilot, smoothed RBF achieved mean RMSE 0.9877 with no negative-$R^2$ failures. Conflicting responses at identical predictor coordinates made exact interpolation unsuitable. All environmental smoothed-RBF fits selected the largest candidate, preventing geometry--smoothing correlation analysis. The findings motivate geometry-aware failure screening but do not establish a transferable rule for smoothing magnitude. Independent multisite validation, appropriate coordinate scaling, joint scale--smoothing tuning, and conditioning diagnostics are needed before an adaptive policy can be claimed.

title: Asymptotic Consistency of a Weighted Nadaraya-Watson Estimator Driven by Fractional Brownian Motion at Random Times
summary: Nonparametric regression conventionally assumes equispaced observations, a premise often violated by empirical data with irregular sampling and long-memory noise. This study establishes the asymptotic mean square ($L^2$) consistency of a weighted Nadaraya-Watson (wN-W) estimator for stochastic processes sampled at random times and perturbed by fractional Brownian motion (fBm). Leveraging the occupation time formula and Fernique's Theorem, we derive exact parametric restrictions on bandwidth and sampling rates ensuring convergence. We validate these theoretical findings via extensive simulations evaluating the mean squared error under varying noise persistence. Crucially, we explicitly benchmark the performance of the estimator under random sampling times against classical deterministic grids, while assessing the relative efficiency of quartic versus Gaussian kernels. Finally, we introduce an interactive Shiny application to dynamically visualize the admissible parameter space, and we empirically validate our theoretical framework by applying the estimator to the Vostok ice core paleoclimatological dataset. This real-world application demonstrates the practical capacity of the methodology to extract macroscopic trends while robustly avoiding severe overfitting under random sampling times.\

title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
summary: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

title: NEVEN: An Open-Source Polyglot Infrastructure Bridging Statistical Computing and Spreadsheet Workflows for Reproducible Research
summary:
We present NEVEN, an open-source infrastructure that embeds R, Julia, Python, Quarto, and JavaScript visualization libraries into Excel through native worksheet formulas. Users run econometric estimators, solve differential equations, and compile reproducible reports using expressions such as =R.MR_Lineal(...), =J.Optimize(...), and =P.ai_call(...), without procedural programming or external application switching. The platform offers over 70 R statistical procedures, 70 high-level Julia procedures backed by more than 200 mathematical functions, and full Python 3 integration for statistical computing and numerical analysis.
  Each language runtime runs in an independent operating-system process connected to the Excel XLL host via Windows Named Pipes and Protocol Buffers. Fatal errors terminate only the affected child process, leaving Excel operational. A static security sandbox checks user code against 25-30 restricted patterns per language, blocking shell execution, file deletion, unauthorized network access, and dynamic evaluation through five bypass-prevention mechanisms validated by 133 tests.
  An embedded WebView2 engine displays interactive Plotly charts, D3.js network and hierarchical visualizations, Leaflet maps, pivot tables, LaTeX notation, PDF documents, and Pluto.jl reactive notebooks through a unified formula, =NEVEN.v(). The docked NEVEN Studio environment offers nine specialized modules, including a Chart Gallery with 325 templates, an in-memory DuckDB SQL console, a retrieval-augmented AI assistant, and a multi-language script editor with English and Spanish localization.
  Econometric estimates match published benchmarks to four decimal places, while Julia linear algebra decompositions achieve machine-precision accuracy (relative error below 10^-14). Released under GNU General Public License v3, NEVEN includes 342 automated unit, property-based, and integration tests.

title: Hypothesis testing for estimable parameters with missing data: available cases or complete cases?
summary: Whether to base inferences on available-case (AC) or complete-case (CC) estimators is a long-standing practical dilemma when data are missing. This issue has been investigated for point estimation in specific problems, but hypothesis testing has received comparatively little attention. The tools needed to address this problem are developed in a fully nonparametric framework for hypotheses concerning parameters that can be estimated through functions of vectors of $U$-statistics, under a MCAR missingness mechanism. The joint asymptotic normality of the AC estimators is established, permitting availability probabilities to vary with the sample size. The limiting covariance matrix factorizes into the complete-data covariance matrix and a matrix determined solely by the availability pattern, with both components admitting consistent estimators. This fact enables the construction of a Wald-type test statistic. The CC approach arises as a special case. These results allow AC and CC based tests to be compared, although the comparison is problem specific, which limits its practical value. Rather than selecting one approach, a test based on the maximum of the two statistics is also considered, whose critical value can consistently approximated by two bootstrap procedures. In simulations, its power lies between those of the AC and CC approaches.

title: Partial pooling beats synthetic respondents as estimators, not as covariates: a preregistered small-sample tournament
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables, supplementary information included. Preregistration: https://osf.io/w6s84. Reproduction package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22793037
summary: Survey estimates for population segments, such as media use by sex and age, rest on few respondents per cell, and a growing literature offers synthetic respondents generated by large language models to fill the gap. That literature has not tested them against the small-area estimators a methodologist would otherwise use. We ran ten estimators, preregistered, on identical household-clustered splits of a Korean media panel across five calibration budgets and three holdout regimes. A multilevel partial-pooling model of the MRP family led every calibration-only estimator at every budget, matching at one hundred respondents what direct estimation reaches with roughly four times as many. On unobserved segments, information fixed as a per-segment prior was inert for synthetic panel and previous wave alike; attached as a bias correction it transferred, at the price of estimation noise. No registered synthetic advantage over MRP survived the paired decision rule. Entered instead as a covariate inside the multilevel model, an exploratory hybrid, the same panel improved on MRP on unobserved segments: the information survives where the registered constructions did not. Interval coverage stayed below nominal throughout and worsened with budget for partial pooling, contrary to prediction.

title: Beyond weak convergence of signed spectral measures: Eigenvector overlaps and high-dimensional prediction risk
summary: Many results in random matrix theory and high-dimensional statistics depend on weak convergence of spectral measures, which is usually established via pointwise convergence of Stieltjes transforms. This approach has recently been applied to signed measures. However, for signed measures, pointwise convergence of Stieltjes transforms alone no longer characterizes weak convergence. While this is unproblematic in many cases, in the high-dimensional regression setting, recently considered by Green and Romanov (2025), the underlying signed eigenvector-overlap measures can fail to converge weakly, despite pointwise convergence of their Stieltjes transforms. Using a novel approach to risk analysis, we show that weak convergence can be replaced by a simple convergence result for bilinear forms. This allows us to establish convergence of the prediction risk for estimators based on arbitrary continuous spectral filters, including (regularized) gradient descent and ridge regression, even when the underlying signed measures fail to converge weakly. Under additional regularity conditions, we construct an explicit finite signed measure yielding an integral representation of the asymptotic prediction risk. This representation provides necessary and sufficient conditions for minimum-norm interpolation and optimally tuned ridge regression to attain the smallest asymptotic prediction risk among estimators with continuous spectral filters. Moreover, we provide characterizations of weak and vague convergence of finite signed measures in terms of pointwise convergence of their Stieltjes transforms.

title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions
summary: Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. However, when multiple sensitive attributes are associated with a data subject, improving fairness with respect to one attribute does not necessarily improve it across all attributes: it may exacerbate disparities associated with other sensitive attributes, including those that are unavailable to the practitioner. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. We characterize these externalities using Wasserstein barycentric disparities and develop a distributional framework that captures changes in both marginal and joint fairness measures. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

title: Estimation and Inference for Multiplicative Error Models via Analytical Derivatives
summary: Maximum Likelihood Estimates (MLEs) of the parameters of a Multiplicative Error Model are typically computed through a standard gradient method, an iterative procedure usually based on numerical approximations to derivatives of the log-likelihood function, owing to the complexity of the analytical derivatives, which involve recursive terms. Building on previous work developed mainly in the GARCH framework, we derive analytical expressions for the score vector and the Hessian matrix of the Multiplicative Error Model log-likelihood by adopting the Gamma distribution for estimation purposes. Then, we illustrate how the iterative algorithm based on the analytical derivatives should be computationally implemented. After maximizing the log-likelihood, we also provide explicit formulas for several estimators of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the MLE. Additionally, we provide analytic formulas for robust covariance estimators that remain valid under distributional misspecification, which are also referred to as the asymptotic variance of the Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator. We also propose a covariance estimator that is consistent under general forms of heteroskedasticity of the error term, while the usually adopted estimators rely on a specific variance assumption. The finite-sample performance of the covariance estimators is assessed through a Monte Carlo investigation. An application on real data completes the analysis.

title: Orthogonal Sparse Subgraph Alignment for Structure-Function Coupling in Brain Networks
comment: 47 pages, 13 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://rampageoppa.github.io/projects/ossa/
summary: Characterizing the relationship between brain anatomical wiring and functional coordination remains a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. This difficulty primarily arises because structure-function coupling in the human brain is spatially heterogeneous, often localized to subnetworks, and inherently difficult to align across disparate representational modalities. We introduce Orthogonal Sparse Subgraph Alignment (OSSA), a principled and interpretable framework designed to identify compact structural cliques that exhibit maximal concordance with functional connectivity (FC) across subjects. Within each FC-derived community, OSSA optimizes an alignment objective over an orthogonal transformation, which absorbs coordinate mismatch between the two connectivity modalities, and a sparse node-selection vector, which identifies the induced structural connectivity (SC) subgraph. Furthermore, for canonical OSSA within a fixed population community, we establish local statistical guarantees under the required assumptions. With high probability, an empirical local maximizer exists in a specified neighborhood of the population target, and every local maximizer in that neighborhood exactly recovers the active support and satisfies a nonasymptotic error bound for the aligned functional projector. Extensive empirical evaluations on simulated data, alongside analyses of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) baseline and longitudinal cohorts, demonstrate that OSSA successfully recovers aligned structural cliques under latent cross-modal rotations. Ultimately, the proposed methodology significantly improves out-of-sample SC-FC alignment over size-matched baselines and identifies compact structural supports with longitudinal consistency in node selection, while multi-support diagnostics suggest a dominant aligned core within the estimated FC communities.

title: Credal Wrapper for Uncertainty Modelling in Sparse Geological Data
summary: Machine learning models for mineral exploration are trained on a few hundred sparse, expensive samples and used to decide where to drill next, so their epistemic uncertainty (EU), the part that more data could remove, matters as much as their predictions. Yet EU cannot be measured on real data, because the counterfactual that defines it is never observed, so estimators are graded by proxies such as out-of-distribution detection and calibration. We contribute a general simulation protocol that makes EU directly computable for a given model and can grade any EU estimator. It separates two estimands the literature conflates, reducible error and estimator spread, builds an oracle reference for each in a synthetic prospectivity field sampled by clustered drilling surveys, and compares uncertainty measures of an identical ensemble within each simulated world. We use it to ask when credal (imprecise-probability) measures are more faithful than Bayesian model averaging (BMA) in the sparse, low-class regime of geological classification. The credal interval width recovers the epistemic ordering better than BMA when members are few, confirming the small-ensemble advantage reported for credal wrappers; the advantage vanishes by M = 10 and reverses at M = 40. Secondly, the choice of credal functional matters more than the choice between credal and BMA. Lastly, the credal advantage does not widen as training data are thinned, so it compensates for few posterior samples rather than few data. On real drill-hole geochemistry from South Australia, a resampling oracle reproduces the first finding. The protocol applies to any EU estimator whose data-generating process can be simulated.

title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
summary: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

title: Don't Match the Noise: Distribution Matching under Unknown Measurement Error with an Audit Sample
summary: Real-world machine learning systems often operate on imperfect measurements: sensors are noisy, annotations are produced by non-experts, and scientific observations are often indirect. In these settings, classic distribution comparison tools such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) can be systematically biased, matching artifacts of the measurement process rather than the underlying mechanisms of interest. We study a practical regime in which noisy observations are abundant, but only a small audited subset contains ground-truth measurements. We propose measurement-error-corrected MMD (MEC-MMD), an audit-based estimator that debiases kernel evaluations without requiring a noise model. MEC-MMD is exactly unbiased for the oracle MMD under simple random auditing, admits an explicit variance decomposition, and is consistent for the population MMD, achieving the standard $O_p(N^{-1/2})$ rate when the audit size scales with the dataset. We demonstrate the utility of distributional matching with MEC-MMD loss for both parameter estimation and unsupervised applications, showing that MEC-MMD consistently outperforms MMD and alternative methods. These results provide a principled foundation for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference, and learning in noisy real-world machine learning pipelines.

title: AIDA: Analysis of Interval Data in R
summary: AIDA is an R package that provides tools for the analysis of interval-valued data, including construction, visualization, robust estimation, and explainable outlier detection. The package is built around the intData class and is designed to support methodological research and applied workflows involving interval-valued data. AIDA implements methods for symbolic covariance estimation based on the Mallows distance, robust estimation via the Interval Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator, and explainable outlier detection using Shapley values. The package also includes visualization tools to support interpretation of the results and several interval-valued datasets.

title: Martingale posteriors for flexible regression via recursive least squares
summary: Predictive Bayes quantifies uncertainty by specifying a sequence of one-step-ahead predictive distributions, inducing a martingale posterior without an explicit prior. Existing parametric constructions rely on stochastic-gradient updates and have seen limited development for flexible regression. We propose a predictive Bayes framework based on recursive least squares, whose martingale posterior has an explicit representation: given future covariates, it is the law of the posterior mean plus a weighted series of independent draws from the standardized predictive distribution. The posterior mean is a penalized least squares estimator, available in closed form and invariant to data ordering, whereas the predictive distribution, for example heavy tailed, is chosen separately without changing the estimator or algorithm. We derive the exact posterior variance under a known design and an asymptotically Gaussian approximation, and obtain the martingale posterior in closed form for Gaussian predictive distributions. Posterior draws are independent by construction, with a known truncation error, and require no Markov chain Monte Carlo. The construction extends to additive, mixed and Gaussian process models. In simulations and an analysis of NHANES triglyceride data, the method attains accuracy comparable to that of a fully Bayesian model with the same response distribution at a fraction of its computational cost.

title: A Goal-Oriented Bayesian Experimental Design to Reduce Uncertainty in Sparse-Angle X-ray Computed Tomography
summary: Sparse-angle X-ray computed tomography (CT) presents a challenge for reliable inference, as limited measurements may leave object boundaries unresolved. Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) methods select informative measurements, but can be computationally expensive or require data-driven surrogates and do not explicitly exploit microlocal visibility. We address this limitation by focusing on estimating inclusion boundaries rather than the entire attenuation field. For piecewise-constant objects, these boundaries correspond to singularities characterized by their wavefront sets. Microlocal analysis determines the X-ray view-angles at which these singularities are visible. We combine this information with Bayesian uncertainty quantification to introduce B-MUSE, a microlocal uncertainty-driven sequential experimental design method. We define a microlocal C-optimality criterion associated with the wavefront direction of the most uncertain boundary singularity and prove that its optimal solution satisfies the microlocal visibility condition. B-MUSE uses this result to sequentially select informative view-angles according to boundary uncertainty. It also incorporates an adaptive stopping criterion that terminates acquisition when additional measurements provide no meaningful uncertainty reduction. We evaluate B-MUSE through numerical experiments, including interpretable examples, prior-generated inclusions, and a multi-inclusion example from an external dataset, and benchmark it against recent methods. The results show that B-MUSE substantially reduces posterior uncertainty with few adaptively selected measurements while providing boundary estimates. These findings establish a direct connection between BOED and microlocal visibility and demonstrate the potential of uncertainty-driven acquisition to reduce measurement requirements for goal-oriented X-ray CT without training data.

title: Statistical-to-computational gaps in central limit theorems for high-dimensional tensors
summary: We study high-dimensional central limit theorems (CLTs) as hypothesis testing problems, comparing the number of summands needed for statistical and computational indistinguishability of the normalized sum from the limiting Gaussian distribution as the dimension and number of summands grow together. For the off-diagonal entries of sums of i.i.d. rank-one tensors formed from standard Gaussian vectors (equivalently, the problem of distinguishing Wigner from Wishart tensors), we prove total variation bounds sharpening previous estimates of Mikulincer (2020) and give matching polynomial-time tests. This shows that the statistical and computational thresholds coincide for this CLT, contrary to a proposal by Kunisky, Moore, and Wein (2024). On the other hand, we also show that, for tensors of order at least three, sufficient Gaussian dilution of the summands by adding independent Gaussian noise and rescaling gives a CLT model with a statistical-to-computational gap (in the above setting and ones with more general rank-one summand distributions). To the best of our knowledge, such a phenomenon has not been observed before in any high-dimensional CLT. In particular, in the relevant parameter regimes, we show that a brute-force search achieves strong detection, while polynomials of degree up to $n^{Ω(1)}$ cannot achieve strong separation. The latter lower bounds control low-degree $χ^2$-divergences by a novel method based on cumulant generating functions, and we further illustrate the use of these tools by applying them to masked tensor CLT models where only a prescribed subset of tensor entries is revealed.

title: Improved last-iterate bounds for SGD with and without replacement
summary: In this work, we study last-iterate convergence bounds for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on convex and $β$-smooth loss functions and improve the bound from $\cO((\log T)^3/T)$ to $\cO((\log T)^3/(T\log\log T))$ in the interpolation regime. The improvement comes from applying a horizon-dependent multiscale estimate of gradients to the comparison of trajectories. The bound applies to both sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement within one pass.

title: Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
summary: Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.

title: Asymptotic Consistency of a Weighted Nadaraya-Watson Estimator Driven by Fractional Brownian Motion at Random Times
summary: Nonparametric regression conventionally assumes equispaced observations, a premise often violated by empirical data with irregular sampling and long-memory noise. This study establishes the asymptotic mean square ($L^2$) consistency of a weighted Nadaraya-Watson (wN-W) estimator for stochastic processes sampled at random times and perturbed by fractional Brownian motion (fBm). Leveraging the occupation time formula and Fernique's Theorem, we derive exact parametric restrictions on bandwidth and sampling rates ensuring convergence. We validate these theoretical findings via extensive simulations evaluating the mean squared error under varying noise persistence. Crucially, we explicitly benchmark the performance of the estimator under random sampling times against classical deterministic grids, while assessing the relative efficiency of quartic versus Gaussian kernels. Finally, we introduce an interactive Shiny application to dynamically visualize the admissible parameter space, and we empirically validate our theoretical framework by applying the estimator to the Vostok ice core paleoclimatological dataset. This real-world application demonstrates the practical capacity of the methodology to extract macroscopic trends while robustly avoiding severe overfitting under random sampling times.\

title: Semiparametric Inference for Marginal Win Odds with Censored Time-to-Event Outcomes
summary: Win statistics provide clinically interpretable measures for comparing treatment groups with prioritized composite outcomes, but efficient covariate-adjustment methods for win statistics with right censored time-to-event outcomes remain limited. We develop a semiparametric framework for marginal win probability and win odds with prioritized time-to-event outcomes, including semi-competing risks, while also accommodating scalar survival outcomes as a special case. The estimand compares independent draws from the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes under treatment and control, which preserves a marginal causal interpretation. We derive the efficient influence function under conditional independent censoring, allowing censoring to depend on baseline covariates and predictable event history. The resulting cross-fitted one-step estimator incorporates covariate adjustment and censoring martingale augmentation, allows flexible estimation of nuisance parameters, and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound under suitable conditions on consistency and convergence rate of nuisance parameters. Simulation studies show that the estimator has small bias, accurate standard error estimation and confidence interval coverage, and substantial efficiency gain relative to the inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted (IPCW) estimator. An application to a randomized breast cancer trial comparing tamoxifen combined with radiotherapy against tamoxifen alone demonstrates improved precision, with an approximately 25\% reduction in estimated variance at five years.

title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: an uncertainty-aware framework, with an application to global cardiovascular disease burden, 1990 to 2023
summary: Modelled health estimates such as those of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study are increasingly used in secondary analyses designed for observed data. However, trajectory clustering typically ignores published uncertainty, selects the number of clusters using criteria blind to it, and assigns countries to groups with unwarranted certainty. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that separates trajectory level from shape, quantifies membership probabilities by perturbing estimates within their uncertainty intervals, selects clusters based on stability under uncertainty, and examines the roles of development, region, and measurement quality. Applied to age-standardised cardiovascular disease DALY rates for 201 countries from 1990-2023 (GBD 2023), the framework identified two stable trajectory types, whereas the gap statistic selected three. The additional cluster was poorly supported (median membership probability 0.70) and disappeared once uncertainty was considered. The retained clusters had similar burdens in 1990 but diverged markedly over time: a stalled-improvement group of 78 countries (median change $-8\%$, 40 of them in sub-Saharan Africa) and a sustained-decline group of 92 countries ($-52\%$). Thirty-one countries remained unclassified because their memberships were uncertain. Results were reproduced using mortality rates, a 2000-2023 analysis window, and bootstrap resampling. Among countries with the narrowest uncertainty intervals, a third well-supported trajectory emerged in former Soviet and Eastern European countries. These findings show that uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters. Ignoring it risks over-interpreting unstable groups and overstating confidence in country classifications. Incorporating published uncertainty and measurement quality should become standard practice when clustering modelled health estimates.

title: Beyond Curvature Bias: Higher-Order Manifold Fitting via Multiscale Cancellation
summary:
Local manifold-fitting procedures smooth noisy observations
  over neighborhoods of scale $h$, inducing a systematic normal bias of order $h^2+σ^2$ that persists at the population level. We develop geometric bias cancellation (GBC), a multiscale framework for higher-order manifold recovery under ambient Gaussian noise. For procedures admitting a normal-bias expansion $c(h,σ)b(x)+O(h^4)$, we construct cross-scale correspondence using estimated normal fibers and show that second-order normal accuracy suffices for fourth-order correspondence accuracy. Canceling the leading geometric bias yields $O(h^4)$ population Hausdorff accuracy while preserving an embedded manifold diffeomorphic to the underlying manifold. We establish the required expansions and finite-sample recovery guarantees for successive tangent-space projection and Gaussian density ridges. For STSP, geometric bias cancellation also achieves an asymptotically vanishing Hausdorff error ratio relative to oracle bandwidth-tuned single-scale fitting. For the local contraction estimator of \citet{yao2023manifold}, we identify an obstruction to scalar bias cancellation and develop a directional cancellation achieving $O(σ^4)$ population Hausdorff accuracy with uniform positive reach, as well as fourth-order finite-sample accuracy when $n\gtrsimσ^{-(d+6)}\log(1/σ)$. Simulations confirm the predicted improvement from second- to fourth-order population bias.

title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Fairness under Data Imbalance: Theory and Adaptive Allocation
summary: Data imbalance across sensitive groups and class labels is common in classification problems and can contribute to substantial fairness disparities. We study how such imbalance affects Equal Opportunity and how synthetic data augmentation can mitigate the resulting unfairness. We first identify two mechanisms, prevalence imbalance and group-size imbalance, through which changes in the training distribution shift the learned decision boundary and induce disparities in group true positive rates. Motivated by this analysis, we study exact full-balance augmentation, which equalizes all group-label cells. We establish conditions under which full balancing strictly improves Equal Opportunity together with a prediction-error comparison under the oracle balanced distribution, and show that the Equal Opportunity gap of the synthetic-data classifier converges to that of the oracle balanced classifier as the sample size grows and the generator error vanishes. The finite-sample convergence rate agrees, up to logarithmic factors and generator-approximation error, with the information-theoretic lower-bound rate under the corresponding regularity regimes. Since exact balancing need not provide the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice, we further propose Accuracy-Constrained Adaptive Synthetic Augmentation (ACASA), which learns both where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated fairness disparity subject to a constraint on predictive accuracy. We provide a finite-sample guarantee comparing the selected augmentation allocation with the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulation studies and real data application support the theoretical findings and demonstrate that synthetic augmentation can substantially reduce fairness disparities while achieving favorable empirical fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

title: GraphInfer: Statistical Inference for Decomposable Graphical Models in R
comment: 44 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. The R package GraphInfer 0.1.0 will be submitted to CRAN; until then, the package and the replication material are available from the author on request
summary: Decomposable graphical models combine closed-form maximum likelihood estimation with local model comparison, which makes structure inference practical with many variables. The R package GraphInfer provides one likelihood framework for decomposable models of continuous, discrete and mixed data, the last as conditional Gaussian models. Structure inference ranges from exact minimum forests and stepwise search to stochastic global search. Nested models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests whose null distributions are exact in finite samples: conditionally on the discrete data for edges with a continuous endpoint, and conditionally on the discrete margins of the smaller model for edges between discrete variables. Missing values are handled by EM, by structural EM, which reuses complete-data searches through a weighted pseudo-sample of expected sufficient statistics, and by multiple imputation; selected models are fit to the observed-data likelihood. The package also treats the graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees: a search over the compatible graphs whose tree moves overcome an obstruction to single-edge moves, fitting of the full accumulation model with measurement noise and bootstrap tests of the accumulation hypothesis. GraphInfer is an independent, pure R successor to the archived package gRapHD. The implementation is validated against independent references, and simulation studies inform its defaults.

title: Beyond weak convergence of signed spectral measures: Eigenvector overlaps and high-dimensional prediction risk
summary: Many results in random matrix theory and high-dimensional statistics depend on weak convergence of spectral measures, which is usually established via pointwise convergence of Stieltjes transforms. This approach has recently been applied to signed measures. However, for signed measures, pointwise convergence of Stieltjes transforms alone no longer characterizes weak convergence. While this is unproblematic in many cases, in the high-dimensional regression setting, recently considered by Green and Romanov (2025), the underlying signed eigenvector-overlap measures can fail to converge weakly, despite pointwise convergence of their Stieltjes transforms. Using a novel approach to risk analysis, we show that weak convergence can be replaced by a simple convergence result for bilinear forms. This allows us to establish convergence of the prediction risk for estimators based on arbitrary continuous spectral filters, including (regularized) gradient descent and ridge regression, even when the underlying signed measures fail to converge weakly. Under additional regularity conditions, we construct an explicit finite signed measure yielding an integral representation of the asymptotic prediction risk. This representation provides necessary and sufficient conditions for minimum-norm interpolation and optimally tuned ridge regression to attain the smallest asymptotic prediction risk among estimators with continuous spectral filters. Moreover, we provide characterizations of weak and vague convergence of finite signed measures in terms of pointwise convergence of their Stieltjes transforms.

title: A Geometric Perspective for Marginal R2: Estimation and Inference in Generalized Linear Mixed Models
summary: Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) are widely used across scientific disciplines, yet quantifying response variation explained by auxiliary information remains challenging for non-Gaussian outcomes and hierarchical dependence. Existing $R^2$ measures provide useful summaries, but their variance-based constructions are not generally linked to a common geometric interpretation, a fixed-design marginal estimand, and corresponding statistical inference. We propose marginal quasi-$R^2$ through two distinct operations. First, marginalization integrates over latent random effects, retaining their uncertainty in the marginal response moments and specifying the model for explanatory assessment. Second, a Quasi-GLM formulation supplies a local working information metric under which orthogonal projection yields an Pythagorean decomposition of explained and unexplained variation. We define a fixed-design population estimand, establish consistency and asymptotic normality of its estimator, and derive cluster-robust sandwich standard errors and confidence intervals under stated regularity conditions. Simulations assess estimation accuracy and interval coverage across response families and random-effects structures. Two ecological applications illustrate the importance of reporting estimation uncertainty alongside marginal quasi-$R^2$. The method is implemented in the R package quasiR2.

title: Hierarchical Empirical-Bayes Forecasting of Sparse Counts with Exposure: An Application to Airline Demand and Premium-Cabin Capacity Sharing
summary: Sparse count forecasting arises when events are rare, exposure varies across observational units, and short histories contain many zeros. Using thin-market airline demand as a motivating application, this paper develops a hierarchical exposure-adjusted Poisson-Gamma (HEPG) framework for probabilistic forecasting. Conditional counts follow a Poisson model with an exposure offset and pooled calendar effects, while unit specific baseline intensities receive a Gamma prior whose hyperparameters are estimated empirically across the population. The resulting posterior is Gamma and the posterior predictive distribution is negative binomial, providing closed-form partial pooling and explicit propagation of parameter uncertainty. This is especially useful for zero-history or low-exposure units, where independent maximum-likelihood estimates are unstable or collapse to zero. An adaptive extension, A-HEPG, adds a moment-matched negative-binomial variance correction when residual extra-Poisson variation remains. In synthetic experiments with 400 heterogeneous markets, HEPG improves average negative log predictive probability relative to complete pooling and independent route-level Poisson estimation. At a mean latent rate of 0.15 requests per exposure unit, the score is 0.525 for HEPG, compared with 0.585 for pooled Poisson and 0.731 for route-level Poisson maximum likelihood. Under strong overdispersion, A-HEPG reduces the score from 0.552 to 0.529. A downstream cabin-capacity example links the predictive distribution to a seat-protection rule based on predictive survival probabilities and fare ratios. The study emphasizes coherent probabilistic inference, partial pooling, and diagnostic model escalation for sparse applied count data.

title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
summary:
Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$.
  For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods.
  In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points.
  We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained.
  We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

title: Nested Ensemble Learning with Topological Data Analysis for Graph Classification and Regression
comment: This is the published version of the article. Published in International Journal of Topology, MDPI, DOI: 10.3390/ijt2040017. Link to the official version: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijt2040017
summary: We propose a nested ensemble learning framework that utilizes Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to extract and integrate topological features from graph data, with the goal of improving performance on classification and regression tasks. Our approach computes persistence diagrams (PDs) using lower-star filtrations induced by three filter functions: closeness, betweenness, and degree2 centrality. To overcome the limitation of relying on a single filter, these PDs are integrated through a data-driven, three-level architecture. At Level-0, diverse base models are independently trained on the topological features extracted for each filter function. At Level-1, a meta-learner combines the predictions of these base models for each filter to form filter-specific ensembles. Finally, at Level-2, a meta-learner integrates the outputs of these filter-specific ensembles to produce the final prediction. We evaluate our method on both simulated and real-world graph datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms base models and standard stacking methods, achieving higher classification accuracy and lower regression error. It also surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, ranking among the top three models across all benchmarks.

title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
summary: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

title: Generalized linear models under distribution uncertainty
summary: In this paper, we study generalized linear models under distribution uncertainty, where the random intercept has mean uncertainty and takes values in an unknown bounded interval. We develop a novel two-step method, named Firth-corrected Expectation-Maximization with Moving Block (FEMMB), to estimate the regression coefficients as well as the lower and upper bounds of the intercept. A Firth bias correction is incorporated into the EM algorithm to mitigate the incidental parameters problem, which is prominent in generalized linear models with many nuisance intercepts. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimated regression coefficients, and the consistency of the estimated intercept bounds. Simulation studies and a real-data application to an imbalanced credit card dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Time-Domain and Spectral Decomposition of Dynamic Coupling with Instantaneous and Time-Lagged Causality: Methodological Evaluation and Application to Cardiovascular Variability
summary: The quantification of dynamic interactions in coupled physiological time series is a central question in biomedical signal processing. A critical issue is the presence of instantaneous dependencies, often neglected in conventional Granger causality (GC) analyses despite potentially reflecting physiologically meaningful effects. We investigate time- and frequency-domain measures of causality within the linear autoregressive (AR) framework, treating instantaneous dependencies according to three formulations: (i) the classical strictly causal AR model, providing spectral measures of time-lagged GC and instantaneous interaction; (ii) the Geweke approach, assigning instantaneous dependencies to the direction opposite to that under investigation; (iii) a single extended AR model incorporating causally-oriented instantaneous dependencies, yielding spectral GC measures accounting for both instantaneous and time-lagged causality. The three approaches are evaluated in simulated Gaussian systems, where dynamic measures can be derived analytically and compared with the expected coupling structure. The single extended AR model emerges as the most consistent formulation when instantaneous dependencies have a physiologically meaningful causal direction and is then applied to cardiovascular interactions between heart period (HP) and systolic (SAP) or diastolic arterial pressure (DAP) in healthy subjects during postural and mental stress. Accounting for instantaneous dependencies substantially affects HP-SAP and HP-DAP interactions, enabling better quantification of baroreflex and cardiac run-off mechanisms and characterization of their responses to stress and of low- and high-frequency dynamics. Overall, the framework provides consistent representation of causal interactions across time and frequency and highlights the importance of accounting for instantaneous dependencies in physiological coupling.

title: Parameter estimation in models with explosive drift and Gaussian noise
summary: We study drift parameter estimation for a positive stochastic process with singular mean-reverting drift driven by Gaussian noise. For Riemann-Liouville fractional Brownian noise with Hurst parameter $H>1/2$, an observable fractional transformation reduces the model to a semimartingale with drift linear in the unknown parameters. Using the quasi-likelihood approach, we derive explicit estimators of both drift coefficients. For a broader class of Gaussian driving processes, we construct a strongly consistent estimator of the ratio $a/b$, which has a natural mean-reversion interpretation, and verify the required assumptions for several Gaussian models. The theoretical results are complemented by a simulation study investigating the effects of the observation horizon and the discretization step on the finite-sample accuracy of the proposed estimators.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Multi-View Clustering via View-Aware Quantization
summary: Federated multi-view clustering (FedMVC) has recently attracted increasing attention for its ability to exploit complementary clustering structures across multiple clients while preserving data privacy. However, existing FedMVC methods often suffer from high communication overhead due to the repeated transmission of high-dimensional representations, which limits their scalability in practical federated systems. Moreover, different views may contribute unequally to the clustering performance, calling for adaptive communication strategies. In this paper, we propose a view-aware quantization algorithm for communication-efficient FedMVC. By dynamically assigning quantization bits based on iteratively updated view importance scores, the proposed algorithm effectively balances clustering performance and communication efficiency under a global bit budget constraint. To validate its generality, we integrate our approach into four state-of-the-art FedMVC methods. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that view-aware quantization achieves up to 6.59x communication reduction while maintaining and in some cases surpassing baseline clustering performance, confirming the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach.

title: Common-DAG Support from Targeted Covariance Changes under Confounding
summary: Targeted covariance changes couple structural rows through a common directed acyclic graph. We study the graph support determined by these experiments when structural errors may be correlated. A positive-gap four-node family has a shortcut identified by common acyclicity. A response indegree of at most two additionally gives unique complete support and two compatible coefficient matrices. The same experiments admit a stable feedback model with the shortcut absent. The result extends to connected graphs with repeated branching and merging. Finite response-column alternatives yield exact bounded-parent compatibility decisions through Horn propagation and partial-target completion. Certified ancestry then supplies an observed-ancestor covariance restriction. Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion reduce inference to a scalar confidence set, and quadratic elimination retains the shared nuisance coefficients with finite-sample edge-error control. In 2048 Gaussian conditions, the scalar procedure reports 127/128 positive edges at gap 1/4 and 524288 observations per cell. Its decisions agree with the joint outer-polynomial reference on the same inputs in all 2022 qualified conditions, with zero reports in 512 null conditions. Exact 16-, 32- and 64-node evaluations verify support and target-coverage conclusions. A root-target characterization connects the identifying information to intervention design.

title: Quantifying Methodological Inflation in Clinical Machine Learning: A Cross-Modality Audit of Subject-Level Leakage and Nested Feature Selection for Parkinson's Disease
summary: Reported accuracy in Parkinson's disease (PD) machine learning can reflect the evaluation protocol rather than real signal. We ask how much evaluation choices inflate performance by comparing naive and rigorous protocols on voice, telemonitoring and blood-transcriptomic datasets. Subject-aware splitting reduced voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780 and telemonitoring R^2 from 0.105 to -0.037; Random Forest recovered neither gap. Supervised probe selection before splitting inflated transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. A nested 50-probe panel matched a 1,000-probe panel (0.811 versus 0.844), and recruitment-wave batch structure was detected. Future work should validate a stable panel on an independent cohort.

title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
summary: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks. For homogeneous linear preferential attachment and Norros--Reittu graphs with Pareto weights, we derive the joint limiting law of the selected rank, retained fraction of the threshold tie, and exponent error. The selector retains of order $n^{2/(α+2)}$ of $n$ vertices, where $α$ is the survival exponent. At this rank, integer spacing and finite-degree departures from a Pareto tail have the same order as sampling fluctuations. The exponent estimate is consistent and retains a shift on the scale used for confidence intervals. For integer degree laws whose tail sums have a first-order inverse-degree expansion, adding the retained tie fraction divided by the threshold to the Hill statistic removes the leading contribution of the tie. Under homogeneous preferential attachment with a fixed known number of edges per new vertex, removing the remaining model-specific term and calibrating for selection gives confidence intervals with asymptotically exact coverage. Observed networks show sensitivity of the fitted exponent and the classification of degree variance to threshold ties. Simulations assess interval coverage and show improved pooled connectivity predictions after correction under both specified graph laws. Changes to the Norros--Reittu weight distribution can reverse the prediction gain.

title: Bet Imaginatively, not Historically in Independent-Data Sequential Testing
summary: Sequential testing avoids some of the many controversies and drawbacks related to traditional batch testing with p-values. In particular, the testing by betting paradigm has developed rapidly in recent years; it frames the level of evidence against the null as the wealth of a player in a betting game. Naturally, how much a player should bet is a key consideration, and should reflect their confidence in what they know about the next observed data point. Much current work uses standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems. In the stochastic setting, where the observed data is independent and stationary, these approaches may be suboptimal. We propose a simple betting strategy, follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE), that exploits the i.i.d. nature of a data stream to estimate the e-power of our current test on the underlying distribution. We average not over the historical evidence collected so far, as generic online learning-based methods do, but instead over the equally-likely possible data sequences we might have seen based on shuffling the data. With an additional principled regularization technique, this simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.
