title: Improving Efficiency and Power in Small Rare-Disease Trials Through Prespecified, Data-Adaptive Covariate Adjustment
summary: Covariate adjustment can potentially improve efficiency in randomized clinical trials, but in rare diseases, limited prior knowledge makes it difficult to specify an adjustment at the design stage. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) with the Super Learner (TMLE+SL) can outperform fixed adjustment methods, such as the G-computation estimator, by leveraging machine learning to learn both the covariates and the functional form of the adjustment from the trial data. Estimating the known treatment mechanism can improve efficiency further. In simulations reflecting real rare-disease trials, TMLE+SL yielded valid inference and achieved greater efficiency and power than conventional analyses. Finally, we also provide practical guidance on specifying TMLE+SL in rare-disease trials.

title: Forecasting Daily Household Electricity Demand in a Hot-Arid City: A Comparative Benchmark of Local, Global, Deep and Foundation Models on ESHED-38
summary: This study benchmarks 24 forecasting configurations on ESHED-38, daily smart-meter consumption for 38 homes in Erbil, Iraq, collected from May 2020 to June 2025 with station weather and a household survey. The configurations span five base families, plus two cross-family ensembles: naive baselines, per-house statistical models, global gradient-boosted trees, global deep networks, and zero-shot time-series foundation models. All are evaluated on the same 54,720 forecasts from 48 weekly origins over a 359-day held-out period, at lead times up to 30 days, using scaled absolute error, the continuous ranked probability score, calibration, and Friedman, Nemenyi and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests. The best configurations cut the scaled error of a seasonal-naive forecast by 20 to 25 percent, and the leading models beat it in all 38 houses. Chronos-2, used without training, is significantly the most accurate model one day ahead; at one week it is statistically tied with TimesFM-2.5, Chronos-Bolt and a pre-specified ensemble, and the two ensembles lead at 30 days. Deep networks trained from scratch do not outperform exponential smoothing on average, and the household survey adds negligible skill. Metered demand peaks in winter and falls as temperature rises. Recorded weather did not improve any model run with and without it. A quality screen helps explain why: on 68 percent of dates a temperature value recurs exactly on other dates, in three annual blocks covering almost all of the test period, suggesting that much of the weather record reuses one annual sequence. The value of weather information is therefore treated as unresolved, and the protocol is released as a baseline.

title: Control Variates to reduce the variance of the empirical Moment Generating Function: an extreme value perspective
summary: Accurate estimation of Moment Generating Functions is fundamental in many applications, but empirical estimators have high variances. Within a control variate setup, Extreme Value Theory is leveraged to identify how extreme values affect the variance reduction method's optimality.

title: Learning Mixtures of Exponential Family
summary: Motivated by causal inference and physical computing systems, we consider the problem of learning mixture of two bounded-support exponential-family distributions with a shared interaction parameter matrix and mixture component-specific linear parameter vectors. The unknown sequence of component labels belongs to a known structured class. We propose an estimator based on a convex loss that avoids the log-partition function; for each fixed label assignment, estimation is a convex optimization problem. We show that the conditional population loss uniquely identifies the interaction matrix and the linear parameter attached to each sample. For a global empirical minimizer, we establish finite-sample bounds on the interaction error in Frobenius norm and the average squared linear-parameter error. The bounds depend on the logarithm of the number of admissible label assignments, and, for fixed dimension and model bounds, imply consistency when this complexity grows sublinearly with sample size. Additional occupancy and separation conditions yield component and label recovery.

title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
summary:
Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$.
  For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods.
  In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points.
  We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained.
  We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

title: Structural Analysis of Object-Valued Time Series
summary: We develop inference for structural patterns in the temporal association of object-valued time series. Our framework is built on pairwise lag profiles, which record the expected value of a chosen pairwise function at each lag and serve as a unified inferential target. We consider three representative structural features: whether a profile reaches stability beyond a finite lag, remains constant over time, and displays geometric regularity at short lags. To assess these properties, we design statistical tests calibrated by a common block multiplier bootstrap that accommodates serial dependence and the overlap inherent in lagged pairs. Gaussian approximation results establish bootstrap validity for asymptotic size control, while suitable signal conditions guarantee consistency against the corresponding alternatives. Finite-sample performance is examined through simulations in both Euclidean and density-valued settings. Applications to electricity load curves and stock-return distributions illustrate how the proposed procedures characterize association across lags.

title: Gaussian processes for real-time urban traffic estimation using a fleet of drones
summary: Real-time urban traffic monitoring is essential for modern city management, yet conventional static sensors provide only limited spatial coverage. Autonomous drone fleets can complement this infrastructure by offering flexible, high-resolution mobile sensing across different parts of the network. This paper introduces a spatio-temporal Gaussian process (GP) framework for reconstructing network-wide traffic states from partial aerial observations. The model accounts for the physical structure of the road network through a graph Matérn kernel, which embeds network topology into the spatial covariance structure, and captures temporal dependencies through an exponential temporal kernel. Within this framework, historical loop detector data provide an informative prior mean that is updated in real time using incoming drone observations, yielding network-wide point estimates together with predictive uncertainty. We validate our framework in two distinct case studies: a microscopic simulation of Barcelona and real-world drone data from Athens. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms historical baselines in estimating and predicting Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT), notably reducing the required fleet size. Furthermore, leveraging the model's predictive uncertainty to guide drone movements yields additional performance gains, highlighting the potential for future uncertainty-aware fleet routing algorithms.

title: Isotonic least squares is robust to heteroscedasticity, unimodal least squares is not
summary: We compare the least squares estimator (LSE) with the $\ell_{1}$-estimator recently introduced by Baraud and Maillard~\citeyearpar{BM-2026} for estimating a regression function under a fixed design, when the errors are independent but possibly heteroscedastic and heavy-tailed. We show that the two estimators coincide on the class of nondecreasing (or nonincreasing) functions on an interval. As a consequence, the isotonic LSE inherits the non-asymptotic $\ell_{1}$-risk bounds of the $\ell_{1}$-estimator, which only require a moment of order $p\in[1,2]$ on the errors and depend on the average of their $p$-th absolute moments rather than on their maximum. This coincidence no longer holds on the nonconvex class of unimodal functions: we exhibit a heteroscedastic Gaussian example in which the LSE is inconsistent while the $\ell_{1}$-estimator converges at the parametric rate. Finally, we show on a one-dimensional linear model that neither estimator dominates the other: depending on the way the noise is distributed among the design points, the LSE may converge at rate $1/n$ while the $\ell_{1}$-estimator is inconsistent.

title: Global-Local and Window-Concatenated Functional Random Forests: Early and Late Fusion of Window-Specific Functional Principal Components
summary: Functional random forests built on a single functional principal component decomposition of the whole domain may dilute features confined to short intervals, whose location is rarely known in advance. We propose two random forests based on window-specific functional principal components. The global-local functional random forest (GL-FRF) is a late-fusion method that stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights; it contains the full-curve forest as a feasible solution, and its weights indicate which parts of the domain drive the prediction. The window-concatenated functional random forest (WC-FRF) is an early-fusion method that trains a single tuned forest on the concatenated window-specific scores. On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve, whereas GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across all 32 simulated and real settings, which makes it the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown.

title: Parameter estimation in models with explosive drift and Gaussian noise
summary: We study drift parameter estimation for a positive stochastic process with singular mean-reverting drift driven by Gaussian noise. For Riemann-Liouville fractional Brownian noise with Hurst parameter $H>1/2$, an observable fractional transformation reduces the model to a semimartingale with drift linear in the unknown parameters. Using the quasi-likelihood approach, we derive explicit estimators of both drift coefficients. For a broader class of Gaussian driving processes, we construct a strongly consistent estimator of the ratio $a/b$, which has a natural mean-reversion interpretation, and verify the required assumptions for several Gaussian models. The theoretical results are complemented by a simulation study investigating the effects of the observation horizon and the discretization step on the finite-sample accuracy of the proposed estimators.

title: FréchetFlow: Flow Matching for Non-Euclidean Data
summary: Scientific observations such as probability distributions, trees and covariance matrices call for generative models that respect their non-Euclidean geometry. While flow matching has been extended to manifolds by utilizing geodesics and velocities, such manifold structures are not available in a general metric space. We introduce FréchetFlow, a generative modeling framework for metric space-valued data that requires neither linear operations nor a smooth manifold structure. A key feature of the proposed approach is that we utilize well-established Euclidean flows to learn the joint distribution of distances to a set of landmarks, whereupon new objects are reconstructed from generated landmark representations. The reconstruction step utilizes weighted Fréchet means of reference objects, drawing on Fréchet regression. We establish Wasserstein error bounds that connect accuracy of the generated object distributions to the placement of landmarks, flow approximation and reconstruction error and prove consistency under finite second moments. This leads to convergence rates that depend on the metric complexity of the target objects, tail moments and fitting accuracy. Experiments show competitive accuracy with established flow matching methods in Euclidean simulations and lower Wasserstein errors than specifically tailored methods for several scientific datasets. Across simulation settings, we find that generation error decreases as sample size increases.

title: Modeling Drug Overdose Mortality Levels Using Social Vulnerability Indicators in U.S. Counties: A Double Machine Learning Approach for Causal Analysis
summary: Drug poisoning mortality (DPM) remains a leading cause of death among working-age Americans, and its burden falls unevenly across communities. Existing county-level studies of social vulnerability and overdose have largely reported predictive or associational relationships, while the shape of the adjusted exposure-response relationship between overall social vulnerability and mortality remains unclear. We examined the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and county drug poisoning mortality across three two-year windows spanning 2016-2021. The associational analysis compared linear regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models of log mortality using period-specific SVI subfeatures and county covariates. The selected XGBoost models were interpreted with SHAP values. The double machine learning (DML) analysis estimated the exposure-response relationship between SVI and DPM and tested the linearity restriction. Socioeconomic vulnerability contributed positively to predicted mortality, with disability and unemployment among the strongest subfeatures, while racial and ethnic minority composition contributed negatively in all three periods. Summing the four theme contributions reduced the overall-index attribution by 34% to 36%, indicating substantial offsetting. Linearity was rejected in every window ($p < 10^{-26}$). The adjusted relationship increased through the middle of the SVI distribution and declined in the upper tail. This pattern remained stable both before and after the outbreak of the epidemic. Overall SVI therefore captured meaningful variation in overdose mortality but did not function as a uniformly increasing risk scale across its full range. Component-level interpretation and current overdose surveillance provide important context for interpreting the composite index.

title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
summary:
We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$.
  Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.

title: Distribution-First Framework for Learning Risk-Sensitive Individualized Treatment Rules
summary: Learning a risk-sensitive individualized treatment rule (ITR) with patient covariates is challenging when the treatment criterion depends on the full conditional outcome distribution rather than only its conditional mean. Existing methods are largely criterion-specific, making it difficult to compare multiple treatment criteria within a common pipeline, such as quantiles, conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and complex preference-based objectives such as cumulative prospect theory. We propose a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning that first estimates treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions and then constructs the target ITR by plug-in criterion evaluation. The proposed framework unifies treatment rule learning across multiple criteria and accommodates hard-to-optimize objectives within the same estimation pipeline. On the theoretical side, it yields a general error propagation result for locally Hölder-stable criteria, linking first-stage distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret, together with sharper regret bounds under standard margin conditions. Empirically, we show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and further evaluate it on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adults.

title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
summary: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks. For homogeneous linear preferential attachment and Norros--Reittu graphs with Pareto weights, we derive the joint limiting law of the selected rank, retained fraction of the threshold tie, and exponent error. The selector retains of order $n^{2/(α+2)}$ of $n$ vertices, where $α$ is the survival exponent. At this rank, integer spacing and finite-degree departures from a Pareto tail have the same order as sampling fluctuations. The exponent estimate is consistent and retains a shift on the scale used for confidence intervals. For integer degree laws whose tail sums have a first-order inverse-degree expansion, adding the retained tie fraction divided by the threshold to the Hill statistic removes the leading contribution of the tie. Under homogeneous preferential attachment with a fixed known number of edges per new vertex, removing the remaining model-specific term and calibrating for selection gives confidence intervals with asymptotically exact coverage. Observed networks show sensitivity of the fitted exponent and the classification of degree variance to threshold ties. Simulations assess interval coverage and show improved pooled connectivity predictions after correction under both specified graph laws. Changes to the Norros--Reittu weight distribution can reverse the prediction gain.

title: Super Learner: A Practical Tutorial
summary: The selection of an optimal predictive model is a pervasive challenge in biostatistics and epidemiology. Relying on a single a priori algorithm risks overfitting and reduced generalizability when applied to new settings. Super Learner is a flexible ensemble machine-learning method that mitigates these risks by combining multiple candidate algorithms into a single prediction model. Using cross-validation, it defines a weighted combination of learners that minimizes a specified loss function, ensuring performance asymptotically equal to or better than the best candidate algorithm. This tutorial provides a comprehensive, practical guide to implementing Super Learner in R for applied researchers. Using a simulated epidemiological dataset with a binary outcome, we demonstrate the step-by-step construction of the ensemble. We cover the foundational statistical concepts, basic implementation, evaluation through cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, feature screening, and performance optimization for metrics such as the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). Additionally, we detail advanced usage, including computational parallelization and the integration of custom algorithms and screening procedures. The guide also includes a consolidated section on best practices for specifying SL, covering loss function selection, effective sample size determination, CV scheme definition, library curation, and discrete vs. ensemble SL decisions, plus a practical reference to the caret package for model preprocessing and comparison. This guide equips epidemiologists and clinical researchers with the tools to confidently incorporate robust machine learning techniques into their predictive modeling workflows.

title: A Hidden Markov Analysis of Wet-Weather Tyre Crossover in Formula One
summary: Detecting a wet-weather regime and deciding when to replace slick tyres are distinct tasks. This study examines their relationship through a retrospective analysis of the 2024 British Grand Prix. A three-state hidden Markov model (HMM) represents normalized lap time and precipitation, while an entry rule requires both a high filtered Wet-state probability and sufficient pace deterioration. The analysis includes 642 car-laps and 33 complete lap-bin observations within the available precipitation record. Each completed-lap signal takes effect on the following lap. The combined rule enters on lap 27, matching the team-weighted modal reference; removing the pace or state condition advances entry to laps 25 and 20, respectively. The combined entry is retained in all 10 team-exclusion refits, but refitting a specification with larger off-diagonal transition probabilities produces entry on lap 20. These comparisons illustrate how state inference can contextualize a performance criterion while exposing dependence on model assumptions. Because estimation and rule development use the same event, the correspondence establishes neither prospective accuracy nor a race-time advantage.

title: Can We Ignore Data Dependence in Inference Implementation? A Positive Answer for Regression Discontinuity Designs
summary: In empirical economics, regression discontinuity design (RDD) inference is commonly based on asymptotic normality under an independence assumption, but the running variables or disturbances may exhibit unknown and complex dependence. We first rigorously identify a fundamental dilemma for this conventional practice. To address it, we propose a validity recovery procedure that redefines the roles of bias and stochastic calibration, thereby decoupling data dependence from stochastic calibration. Taking the independence-assumption-based confidence interval as our inferential anchor, our procedure restores its validity while preserving its asymptotic leading constant, even when the data are dependent. For fixed-design RDD based on local linear regression, our intervals achieve asymptotically exact nominal coverage and, compared with the anchor, exploit higher-order smoothness without enlarging the asymptotic variance constant, attaining the minimax-optimal shrinking rates up to a mild factor, such as $\sqrt{\log T})$. The procedure requires neither specific dependence frameworks (e.g., mixing or physical dependence) nor dependence-modeling techniques (e.g., long-run variance estimation). For random-design RDD, under more specific dependence assumptions, we derive the rate-explicit coverage error at each nominal level and characterize the trade-off between this rate and interval length. Moreover, modeling dependence becomes an optional enhancement that can further enable validity recovery and improve finite-sample coverage, while averaging over repeated calibrations stabilizes the randomized center and protects against undercoverage in finite samples without increasing interval length. In short, under mild dependence and moment conditions, our procedure makes data independence an implementation default rather than a validity requirement. Simulations support the theoretical results.

title: When and How SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Functional Scaling Law Perspective
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a spotlight paper
summary: We study how the sign operator interacts with gradient noise to shape the learning dynamics and scaling behavior of sign-based optimizers. In power-law kernel regression with diagonal features, we establish a functional scaling law (FSL) for SignSGD under general learning rate schedules. The FSL describes the learning dynamics through two processes: signal learning and noise forgetting. The key mechanism is noise-induced preconditioning: gradient noise smooths the sign operator, inducing an effective preconditioned SGD. Noise-curvature alignment enables this preconditioning to transform the effective Hessian from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{H}^{1/2}$. The resulting dynamics exhibit faster signal learning but slower noise forgetting than SGD. This tradeoff yields a regime-dependent comparison with SGD: (i) SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; (ii) both optimizers achieve the same data efficiency in the easy-task regime, but SignSGD maintains this efficiency at larger batch sizes, requiring fewer optimization steps for a fixed data budget. Power-law kernel regression experiments support the proposed mechanism and predicted scaling behavior. LLM pre-training experiments further suggest that the SignSGD FSL better captures the batch-size dependence of loss dynamics for sign-based optimizers than the original SGD FSL.

title: Can a search hold its own bar? In-loop deflation and its exploits in autonomous strategy discovery
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21725589
summary: Corrections for backtest overfitting such as the deflated Sharpe ratio are applied after a search ends: the searcher maximises raw performance and a separate procedure deflates the reported winner. Autonomous searches driven by large language models perform many implicit backtests before reporting, so this paper asks what changes when the correction moves inside the loop and the acceptance threshold is indexed to the running count and dispersion of the search's own trials. The threshold then becomes an object the search can optimise against: we show analytically that a naive in-loop bar admits a variance-dilution effect, in which mediocre near-duplicate candidates lower the bar because the ledger's dispersion falls faster than its trial-count factor grows. We propose two defences, a pre-registered variance floor and a monotone high-water-mark bar, and evaluate the construction under a protocol frozen before any run, with every in-loop decision replaying exactly from its recorded trace. Across 53 audited hundred-candidate searches over two frontier models, two universes, and two feature spaces, the gated search reports "no certifiable discovery" on 36 of 37 runs, un-gated controls report a strategy on all 16, and every arm's out-of-sample confidence interval includes zero. Supporting studies find that state-based stopping reaches the same outcome after 8 to 9 trials at about a twelfth of the trial budget while an adaptive budget adds nothing, that a controlled stress test reproduces the dilution effect and both defences, and that a hundred nominal trials collapse to 6 to 8 effectively independent return streams. We scope these results to the analysed system.

title: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
summary: We propose Fréchet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fréchet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fréchet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

title: Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition: Information, Uncertainty, and Conditional Regime Inference
summary: When do mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes? Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD) fits joint regime laws on signed KMD mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions. For centered Gaussian regimes with independently varying known noise variances, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior precisely when all classes share their cross-covariances and class variances can differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph. We extend the characterization to nonzero means and show that freely varying correlated noise forces a fixed linear log-odds decoder to retain the full quadratic feature span even for two distinct centered regimes. At fixed quality, a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis. Its smallest Bayes log-loss gap over bases of condition number at most $κ$ has sharp order $κ^{-1}$. Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. Two controlled experiments with 64 independent panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls and depends on how the competing point rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
summary: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
summary: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

title: On Ignorability Beyond Missing at Random: Completion-Invariant Missingness for Nonmonotone Missing Data
summary: The missing-at-random assumption underlies most analyses of incomplete data. Under nonmonotone missingness, it is especially stringent, imposing pattern-specific restrictions with different conditioning sets. A strictly weaker normalization condition is known to justify maximizing the observed-data likelihood. We show that every law satisfying this condition has a unique missing-at-random counterpart sharing its observed-data and complete-data distributions. Observed-data procedures developed under missing at random for identified functionals, including doubly robust estimators, therefore remain valid, with the same semiparametric efficiency bound. We then prove that the condition holds if and only if filling in the missing values from their conditional distribution under the true full model preserves the complete-data distribution, hence the name completion-invariant missingness. We use a characteristic kernel to compare the completed distribution with the fitted model and assess the joint compatibility of the specified full model and completion-invariant missingness. We derive the asymptotic null distribution with estimated parameters and establish bootstrap and multiplier calibration. Since a parametric full model alone need not identify completion-invariant missingness, we give identification conditions for Gaussian, Student $t$ and finite mixture families. Simulations assess sensitivity to departures from each assumption, and applications to clinical laboratory measurements and childhood growth illustrate the diagnostic.

title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity
comment: 31 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code and results: https://github.com/YYKKCC-kevin/watermark-prevalence
summary: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
summary:
We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$.

In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.

title: Regularized trimmed Factorial and Reduced K-means for contaminated high-dimensional data: separating geometry, search and selection
summary: Factorial and Reduced K-means estimate a partition and a low-dimensional clustering subspace jointly, which makes them attractive when the variables that separate groups are not those that dominate total variance. On contaminated high-dimensional data they face three linked problems: trimming can make the scatter matrices singular, the criterion has many local optima, and the rank, number of groups and trimming proportion are unknown and interact. We propose REG-HD-TFKM and REG-HD-TRKM, regularized trimmed versions of the two methods, together with a selection procedure that handles these problems as separate decisions. A ridge-stabilized spectral step keeps every fit well defined; heterogeneous multistart search explores alternative solutions; method-specific agreement and reproducibility scores choose among them; and trimming is applied only when a radial diagnostic or the path over trimming levels supports it. A simulation study with 41 design cells shows why the separation matters. Two representations of euro-area bank balance sheets show that similar partitions can rest on nearly orthogonal subspaces, and that the same selected structure can describe different retained samples.

title: Bayesian Evidence Fusion for Capability Tracking-A Simulation Study and Historical CI Pilot
summary: SaaS capability assessments can become stale between questionnaires, while delivery telemetry offers incomplete and correlated evidence. Continuous assessment and Bayesian delivery analysis already exist, leaving uncertainty about how biased surveys and missing observations should influence capability estimates.We implement SAAS-MATURITY-TWIN, an anchored Gaussian state model that jointly filters capability proxies and persistent survey offsets. Source covariance prevents correlated observations from being counted independently. Conditional uncertainty supports forecasting and budgeted intervention screening, with action effects estimated from randomized synthetic cohorts. Ten seeds generate forty paired worlds spanning reference observations, extensive missingness, informative missingness, and increased noise. Reference latent root mean squared error is 0.1261, compared with 0.1452 for a tuned moving average; nominal ninety percent intervals cover 90.3 percent. Improved state recovery produces only small incident forecasting differences. Adaptive conformal inference and an adapted conformal PID controller are evaluated separately for observed telemetry, where noise shifts expose calibration limitations. A licensed TravisTorrent pilot evaluates build prediction on 13 074 held out builds from 224 projects. Logistic regression achieves a Brier score of 0.1289, close to random forests. These results support reproducible methodological testing, but do not establish real organizational maturity, intervention effectiveness, or production readiness. Independent calibration and longitudinal validation remain necessary.

title: Unequal-probability distributional balance and the Horvitz-Thompson estimator
summary: Auxiliary information can improve estimation precision under probability sampling, but the relationship between the study and auxiliary variables may not be known well enough to specify suitable balancing variables. Distributionally balanced designs address this by targeting agreement between sample and population auxiliary distributions. We extend energy-based distributional balance to prescribed unequal inclusion probabilities by comparing the empirical sample distribution with an inclusion-probability-weighted population distribution. Under a regularity condition relating the study values divided by their inclusion probabilities to the auxiliaries, we establish an upper bound on the design variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator in terms of the expected energy distance. This bound motivates an algorithm that exchanges units between randomly paired candidate samples without increasing their average energy distance. Combined with random initialization and uniform selection of a final candidate, the procedure preserves the prescribed first-order inclusion probabilities. We evaluate its auxiliary-space properties and estimation performance using generated populations and the Meuse data.

title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing
summary: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.

title: Can We Ignore Data Dependence in Inference Implementation? A Positive Answer for Regression Discontinuity Designs
summary: In empirical economics, regression discontinuity design (RDD) inference is commonly based on asymptotic normality under an independence assumption, but the running variables or disturbances may exhibit unknown and complex dependence. We first rigorously identify a fundamental dilemma for this conventional practice. To address it, we propose a validity recovery procedure that redefines the roles of bias and stochastic calibration, thereby decoupling data dependence from stochastic calibration. Taking the independence-assumption-based confidence interval as our inferential anchor, our procedure restores its validity while preserving its asymptotic leading constant, even when the data are dependent. For fixed-design RDD based on local linear regression, our intervals achieve asymptotically exact nominal coverage and, compared with the anchor, exploit higher-order smoothness without enlarging the asymptotic variance constant, attaining the minimax-optimal shrinking rates up to a mild factor, such as $\sqrt{\log T})$. The procedure requires neither specific dependence frameworks (e.g., mixing or physical dependence) nor dependence-modeling techniques (e.g., long-run variance estimation). For random-design RDD, under more specific dependence assumptions, we derive the rate-explicit coverage error at each nominal level and characterize the trade-off between this rate and interval length. Moreover, modeling dependence becomes an optional enhancement that can further enable validity recovery and improve finite-sample coverage, while averaging over repeated calibrations stabilizes the randomized center and protects against undercoverage in finite samples without increasing interval length. In short, under mild dependence and moment conditions, our procedure makes data independence an implementation default rather than a validity requirement. Simulations support the theoretical results.

title: The predictive discrepancy: an objective Bayes criterion for constructing calibrating priors
summary: We construct objective priors for regular univariate parametric models designed to produce low coverage probability bias of Bayesian predictive distributions, giving rise to calibrated prediction in repeated use. This is achieved by defining the predictive discrepancy and deriving a class of minimum predictive discrepancy priors. In the multiparameter case these priors will often be data-dependent. The predictive efficacy of alternative global priors can be assessed by comparison with these priors. The effectiveness of the theory is illustrated by a number of examples.

title: Modelling the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related home insurance claims
summary: We study the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related claims in private home insurance, combining detailed portfolio and claim information with publicly available high-resolution weather data. Existing approaches typically start from an identified severe weather event, such as a hailstorm, and model the dynamics of the claims caused by that event. In practice, however, claims arise under moderate as well as severe conditions, and the claims handling process runs continuously. An insurer therefore requires insight into the occurrence and reporting of claims on every calendar day. Modelling all calendar days jointly poses two challenges: recently occurred claims are only partially reported, and days with severe weather are rare while accounting for a large share of the claims. We propose a multi-regime EM-XGBoost framework that addresses both: an expectation-maximisation setup accounts for the incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims, while a data-driven regime structure lets the occurrence and reporting dynamics differ across weather conditions. In a case study on a Dutch home insurance portfolio, we compare single- and two-regime specifications for two spatial resolutions: the country as a whole, and its individual regions. We find that the regional two-regime model outperforms the regional single-regime model as well as both national models, indicating that the benefit of a multi-regime setting depends on a sufficiently granular spatial resolution. We also show that daily covariates constructed from hourly weather observations, capturing the duration and the intra-day timing of severe weather, improve both the occurrence and the reporting model.

title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
summary: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

title: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
summary: We propose Fréchet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fréchet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fréchet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

title: Causal invariance and identifiability for interventions in multi-state models
summary: We propose an identification theory for stochastic interventions on the transition dynamics in continuous-time multi-state models. Interventions are formalized as local modifications of a likelihood satisfying a causal invariance property. We show that identification from observed data is achieved when no unmeasured process simultaneously affects an intervened local characteristic and a competing or subsequent non-intervened local characteristic, covariate local characteristic, or censoring intensity. Our framework allows for intervening on both the timing and type of events, accommodates measured and latent covariates as time-varying marked point processes, and extends to right-censored data. We exemplify by considering identifiability in two concrete applications: one studying the effect of changing the timing of intrauterine insemination on the probability of pregnancy, and one studying the effect of changing the type of dysphagia relieving surgery on the risk of death in esophageal cancer patients.

title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.

title: Common-DAG Support from Targeted Covariance Changes under Confounding
summary: Targeted covariance changes couple structural rows through a common directed acyclic graph. We study the graph support determined by these experiments when structural errors may be correlated. A positive-gap four-node family has a shortcut identified by common acyclicity. A response indegree of at most two additionally gives unique complete support and two compatible coefficient matrices. The same experiments admit a stable feedback model with the shortcut absent. The result extends to connected graphs with repeated branching and merging. Finite response-column alternatives yield exact bounded-parent compatibility decisions through Horn propagation and partial-target completion. Certified ancestry then supplies an observed-ancestor covariance restriction. Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion reduce inference to a scalar confidence set, and quadratic elimination retains the shared nuisance coefficients with finite-sample edge-error control. In 2048 Gaussian conditions, the scalar procedure reports 127/128 positive edges at gap 1/4 and 524288 observations per cell. Its decisions agree with the joint outer-polynomial reference on the same inputs in all 2022 qualified conditions, with zero reports in 512 null conditions. Exact 16-, 32- and 64-node evaluations verify support and target-coverage conclusions. A root-target characterization connects the identifying information to intervention design.

title: On Ignorability Beyond Missing at Random: Completion-Invariant Missingness for Nonmonotone Missing Data
summary: The missing-at-random assumption underlies most analyses of incomplete data. Under nonmonotone missingness, it is especially stringent, imposing pattern-specific restrictions with different conditioning sets. A strictly weaker normalization condition is known to justify maximizing the observed-data likelihood. We show that every law satisfying this condition has a unique missing-at-random counterpart sharing its observed-data and complete-data distributions. Observed-data procedures developed under missing at random for identified functionals, including doubly robust estimators, therefore remain valid, with the same semiparametric efficiency bound. We then prove that the condition holds if and only if filling in the missing values from their conditional distribution under the true full model preserves the complete-data distribution, hence the name completion-invariant missingness. We use a characteristic kernel to compare the completed distribution with the fitted model and assess the joint compatibility of the specified full model and completion-invariant missingness. We derive the asymptotic null distribution with estimated parameters and establish bootstrap and multiplier calibration. Since a parametric full model alone need not identify completion-invariant missingness, we give identification conditions for Gaussian, Student $t$ and finite mixture families. Simulations assess sensitivity to departures from each assumption, and applications to clinical laboratory measurements and childhood growth illustrate the diagnostic.

title: Robust Tests for Heteroskedasticity in Nonparametric Regression under Covariate-Dependent Higher-Order Moments
comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. This preprint contains the main article only; supplementary technical proofs and additional simulation and empirical analyses are not included
summary: We propose Cramér--von Mises- and Kolmogorov--Smirnov-type tests of constant conditional variance in nonparametric regression. The test statistics are constructed from a third-order $U$-process and remain valid when higher-order features of the conditional error distribution vary with the covariates. We derive their limiting distributions under the null hypothesis and study their asymptotic behavior under fixed alternatives and Pitman-type local alternatives. A multiplier bootstrap procedure calibrates the critical values, and Monte Carlo experiments show that the proposed tests have rejection frequencies close to the nominal level in the simulation designs. An application to the National Child Development Study provides evidence of heteroskedasticity in pooled weekly earnings. In the male hourly-earnings sample, rejecting a stronger error-distribution restriction does not entail rejecting homoskedasticity.

title: Where Does EEG Sleep-Onset Forecasting Skill Arise? A State-Conditioned Evaluation
summary: Sleep is scored afterwards in 30-second epochs as wake (W), the transitional stage N1, or N2. We study EEG forecasts, issued every 30 s from the preceding 30 s of EEG alone, of whether the first scored N2 epoch will begin within five minutes, on Sleep-EDF. A Brier score pooled over decisions made before and after the input is scored N1 does not show when the gain arose. In our own prespecified one-shot held-out comparisons, the spectral model SpecLR-18 improved on a training prevalence constant by 18.3% in the internal test, whereas its prespecified external result was inconclusive. Joining the retrospectively scored stage of each input epoch to the same frozen predictions, almost all of that internal-test Brier difference was attributed to N1-scored decisions; a diagnostic reference told only the scored stage reached 26.3% in the internal test and 29.5% in the external cohort, above the spectral forecasts in point estimate though not every difference excluded zero; and within-stage EEG advantages seen in single cohorts were not consistent across cohorts, with no consistent wake-stratum improvement. These references use labels unavailable online and cannot reveal what a model represents; they show why pooled forecasting scores need state-conditioned interpretation before being read as early anticipation.

title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
summary: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

title: Sliced Inverse Regression Revisited: When the Number of Predictors Grows Proportionally With the Sample Size
summary: Li (1991) introduced sliced inverse regression (SIR) as a dimension reduction method and established its theoretical properties under the assumption that the number of predictors $p$ remains fixed as the sample size $n$ tends to infinity. In this paper, we revisit the theoretical properties of SIR in the high-dimensional regime where $p/n \to γ\in [0,1)$, assuming normally distributed predictors and a fixed number of slices. We show that the sample SIR eigenvalues exhibit an upward bias when $γ>0$, that their fluctuations are governed by the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble, and that the signal eigenvalues are asymptotically normal after an appropriate bias correction. We demonstrate that Li's chi-squared test requires a scaling adjustment to achieve the nominal asymptotic size when $γ>0$. We further propose two additional tests that achieve the nominal asymptotic size: an exact test based on Li's test statistic and a largest-eigenvalue test. In addition, we derive closed-form limits for the accuracy of the estimated SIR directions and show that their first-order expansions in $γ$ agree with Li's approximation. Finally, we establish the limiting distribution of the estimated sufficient predictors for a new observation and show that, when $γ>0$, they contain an additional independent Gaussian noise component. Simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings.

title: Methodological Pitfalls in Predicting Ship Turnaround Time at Brazilian Ports: An Empirical Audit and a Reproducible Pipeline
summary: Two recent studies on ship turnaround time at Brazilian ports report models with R-squared scores above 0.80 on data from the national waterway transportation agency. We audit their published datasets and reveal these results are inflated by structural data leakage. Specifically, 97 percent of berthing events in their random row-level split appear in both training and testing partitions. We demonstrate that a model's R-squared drops from 0.82 to 0.20 when the data is properly split at the berthing level. We further document additional methodological flaws, including survivorship bias, undocumented target truncation, and the retention of variables that algebraically reconstruct the target. To address these issues, we propose a reproducible pipeline that aggregates cargo to the berthing level, utilizes conditional imputation, and represents high-cardinality cargo variables through weighted averages of multilingual sentence embeddings. Evaluating six time targets and thirty seeds, our pipeline reveals that cargo embeddings yield statistically significant improvements on four operational targets, while administrative waiting times remain unaffected. Prior works missed this per-target heterogeneity by conflating genuine signal with leaked identity.

title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

title: Conformal prediction for censored life history data
summary: We consider individual prediction of general summaries of a multistate trajectory, such as time alive out of hospital or time spent in remission. Right censoring complicates calibration because these outcomes may be only partially observed. We develop a conformal prediction approach for scalar and vector summaries over a fixed clinical horizon supported by follow-up. For each candidate region, we define the coverage determining time as the earliest time at which the observed history establishes whether the outcome lies in the region, even if the outcome itself is still unknown. We weight observed coverage decisions by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored to that time and augment the estimator with conditional coverage probabilities for unresolved histories. For a fixed region, the coverage estimator is doubly robust with respect to the censoring and conditional coverage models and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are consistent at suitable rates. For the calibrated region, we derive a finite-sample lower bound on the coverage probability and establish asymptotic validity if either model is correct. In simulations, using partial histories yields narrower prediction intervals at comparable coverage. We illustrate joint prediction of days in and out of hospital in the HF-ACTION trial and prediction of relapse-free time in the German Breast Cancer Study Group cohort.

title: Can Model Answer Probabilities Represent Survey Populations? Conditional Prediction and Joint Validity in Jev Survey Simulation
summary: Survey simulations require realistic combinations of answers, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish that a model can generate them. We evaluate the option probabilities returned by Jev, a TypeSafe decision model, using linked responses to 20 binary items from five archived survey waves. We compare population-only prediction, prediction given recorded answers, and sequential completion that uses generated answers to predict later responses. Joint comparisons hold the starting population information fixed, and two three-question cases are completed in both question orders. We evaluate predictive scores, answer frequencies, and associations against the survey records. Recorded answers can improve predictive scores while associations remain distorted. Large conditional errors also occur. For example, among men who described themselves as having traditional values, the model predicted that 16% would see men and women as similar in workplace abilities, compared with 56% in the survey. Sequential completion has mixed effects on joint validity, and reversing question order produces different joint distributions in both tested cases. Order checks and classical marginal bounds clarify what can be assessed before linked validation answers are available. The findings support validating the joint events a simulation uses and separating empirical constraints from model assumptions. The evidence concerns selected binary tasks and one model version.

title: A Latent Semiparametric Mixture Model for Robust Heterogeneity Learning in High Dimensions
summary: Learning heterogeneity from high-dimensional data has become a fundamental task across many data-driven fields. Cluster analysis is a widely used unsupervised tool for this purpose, and many existing methods have been adapted to high-dimensional settings through sparsity constraints. In contrast to algorithmic approaches, model-based clustering offers clean theoretical guaranties and computational simplicity, but can be restrictive in practice due to its reliance on specific parametric distributions. We propose a novel latent semiparametric mixture model for clustering, in which the observed data follow a Gaussian mixture after latent coordinate-wise monotone transformations. Furthermore, assuming a sparse optimal clustering rule in the latent space, we develop a new method, CESME, tailored for high-dimensional clustering. By allowing unspecified transformations, our framework becomes substantially more flexible and robust than traditional model-based approaches. The clustering error of CESME is shown to approach the optimal clustering error at a rate matching that obtained when the true transformations are known. Extensive simulations and real data analysis confirm that CESME outperforms a broad range of existing high-dimensional clustering methods, including those designed for single-cell RNA sequencing data. The online supplementary file contains technical proofs, additional discussions, and more numerical results.

title: Data augmentation for the generalizability and transportability of fairness in a clinical heart failure algorithm
summary: Synthetic data augmentation has been proposed as a way to artificially supplement clinical datasets to address fairness concerns in downstream classification algorithms. This approach is closely related to upweighting or upsampling methods employed for the problem of class imbalance, which have shown mixed empirical results in practice. Synthetic data augmentation also runs the risk of overfitting to the noise present in subgroups with relatively small sample sizes, raising both generalizability and transportability concerns. We present an empirical evaluation of synthetic data augmentation for fairness in tabular data using simulation studies as well as a real-world application of in-hospital mortality classification for heart failure patients in two distinct data samples. We implement upsampling and upweighting methods as benchmarks for the implicit fairness objective of synthetic data augmentation. Our results suggest that the fairness impacts of data augmentation are sensitive to the design of the downstream algorithm as well as the deployment context and its similarity to the training data. It is crucial that studies making generalizability and transportability claims should provide empirical support for these assertions.
