title: Tests of Covariate Effects and Model Selection in Finite Mixture Regression Model
summary: Finite mixture regression models are widely used to capture the heterogeneous effects of covariates on a response variable. Our study, motivated by the analysis of Chiroptera, explores the dynamic effects of various environmental, biological, and human-related covariates on the evolutionary development of bat forearm using finite Gaussian mixture regression (GMR) models. In this paper, we address two key questions: (1) which covariates are associated with the variation in forearm length; and (2) whether the associated covariates have the same effect across all subpopulations. To answer these questions, we propose two stepwise procedures within the finite GMR framework based on the weighted significance test (WEST): (1) a stepwise variable selection procedure to identify relevant influential covariates, and (2) a stepwise effect-type determination procedure to determine each relevant covariate as having either a homogeneous or heterogeneous effect across subpopulations. Based on these procedures, we introduce a stepwise model selection procedure for finite mixture regression, illustrated through finite GMR models. Simulation studies are conducted to assess the performances of our proposed procedures. The proposed procedure will be applied to the Chiroptera dataset.

title: Empirical Bayes mirror testing for persistent widening of achievement gaps in U.S. school districts
summary: Unequal recovery from pandemic learning losses raises concerns about widening achievement gaps between economically disadvantaged students and their peers. This study seeks to identify districts whose mathematics gaps widened in every annual interval from 2022 to 2025. The analysis uses estimates from the Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA) for 5,600 U.S. school districts. Identifying such districts requires accounting for correlated errors and differing precision in the estimated annual changes, as well as multiplicity. The true annual gap changes in each district form an effect vector, and persistent widening means that every component is positive. To address this class of multiple testing problems, we propose an empirical Bayes mirror procedure. It uses an estimated distribution of effect vectors to guide ranking and covariance-adjusted mirror observations to calibrate selection. The procedure achieves finite-sample false discovery rate (FDR) control under a Gaussian observation model, without requiring accurate estimation of the posterior null probabilities used for ranking. Simulations demonstrate power gains from incorporating information about the distribution of effect vectors. At a target FDR of 25%, the SEDA analysis identifies eight districts in five states with evidence of widening gaps in every annual interval.

title: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
summary: We propose Fréchet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fréchet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fréchet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

title: A Proper Random Walk Spline Model for Bayesian Smoothing
summary: We introduce the Proper Random Walk (PRW) family of spline models with a particular focus on the Second-Order Proper Random Walk (PRW2), a proper stationary alternative to the standard random walk of order 2 (RW2) spline. The PRW2 retains the computational strengths and spline-like smoothing of the RW2 while providing uniform marginal variance and stable uncertainty behavior. The PRW2 model is governed by a range parameter that controls correlation decay: in the infinite-range limit, it recovers RW2. In addition to its discrete representation, we show that the PRW2 model admits a continuous-time formulation as the critically damped Matérn model with smoothness $ν=3/2$, which provides an interpretable parameterization and enables construction through a Galerkin finite-element approximation on general grids. To mitigate edge distortions on bounded domains, we propose a local boundary correction that enforces the stationary joint law while preserving sparsity and $O(n)$ factorization. Finally, we develop penalized complexity priors for the model hyperparameters, enabling principled shrinkage toward the RW2 limit. The model is applied to simulated and real data to illustrate its properties and advantages.

title: GrAFT-PDX: Growth and Failure-Time Modeling of Patient-Derived Xenograft Experiments
summary: Cancer drugs are often evaluated for efficacy in mice before proceeding to human clinical trials. To do this, human tumors are engrafted onto immune-incompetent mice to create a patient-derived xenograft (PDX). Engrafted tumors can be propagated to evaluate multiple drugs, but the time and costs involved in PDX studies limit high throughput drug screens in mice. Here we present GrAFT-PDX, a Bayesian model of PDX drug screens that aims to reduce the PDX screening burden by enabling imputation of missing experiments and early stopping of likely unsuccessful drugs. Unlike conventional survival or growth models, GrAFT-PDX jointly predicts tumor growth and survival outcomes using a learned latent function decomposition. In experiments on a large-scale PDX dataset, GrAFT-PDX outperforms Cox proportional hazards models at predicting time of death, outperforms machine learning baselines at predicting tumor growth, and recovers known gene-treatment relationships without genomic input.

title: A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
summary: Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the "effect hierarchy principle"). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

title: Bounded Metrics for Probability Measures on the Sphere
summary: Directional distributions can have the same normalized mean direction while differing substantially in shape. Comparing them requires a distance whose response to geometric displacement and probability overlap matches the statistical question. We examine ten bounded metrics or metric families for probability measures on the sphere, scaling each to have maximum value one, covering transport, sliced transport, kernel and energy distances, and comparisons based on probability mass. We explain which metrics describe weak convergence, which admit Hilbert-space norm representations, and which pairs attain the maximum distance. Examples and counterexamples show how these distinctions affect empirical comparisons and numerical approximations. A summary table and relationship diagram support the choice of a distance. The discussion separates exact metrics from finite representations, unbiased estimators, and regularized transport costs.

title: Is generative AI really changing public sector work? Evidence from a multi-country survey
summary: Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform how public services are delivered, with important implications for public service productivity. But how widely is the technology actually being used - and is it making any difference? Our survey of 3,362 public sector workers across the UK, the USA, South Africa and the EU finds widespread use of AI in every region. Our findings suggest that this spread is being driven by bottom-up individual adoption rather than top-down institutional adoption. In the EU, for example, 65\% of respondents use AI, while only 19\% say their organisation has formally adopted it. Most users are positive about its effects, with 79\% saying AI has improved their productivity. However, only 29\% say it has increased what is expected of them at work, raising questions about how truly transformative the technology is so far. Across regions, South Africa is a clear outlier, with the highest levels of use, organisational adoption, optimism and awareness of guidelines.

title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
summary:
Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$.
  For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods.
  In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points.
  We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained.
  We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

title: Clustering professional football players using Gaussian mixture models: A case study of the English Premier League 2024/25
summary: The increasing availability of detailed football performance data has created new opportunities for identifying player archetypes and informing recruitment and tactical decision-making. Most existing clustering approaches assign each player to a single group, despite the reality that many modern footballers perform hybrid roles spanning multiple stylistic categories. Performance data for 314 outfield players from the 2024/25 English Premier League season are analysed using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) applied to principal component representations of player statistics. Unlike hard-assignment methods such as k-means, the GMM provides probabilistic cluster memberships, allowing uncertainty and role hybridity to be quantified. Seven player archetypes are identified in the full dataset. Posterior membership probabilities reveal a subset of players whose profiles span multiple clusters, providing an objective measure of tactical flexibility and stylistic ambiguity. Further analyses within defender, midfielder, and forward groups recover position-specific sub-archetypes and highlight exceptional outliers. The results demonstrate that model-based clustering provides a flexible and interpretable framework for identifying latent structure in high-dimensional performance data while explicitly quantifying uncertainty in cluster membership. More broadly, the approach is readily transferable to other sports and domains in which individuals exhibit overlapping characteristics and cannot be adequately represented by hard cluster assignments alone.

title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
summary:
We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$.
  Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.

title: Testing Conditional Mean Independence
summary: This article introduces a novel nonparametric test for conditional mean independence, which formally evaluates whether a random vector X has an additional impact on the mean regression function of a response Y when a conditioning random vector Z is already included. By framing the problem as classical partial effect testing, our approach goes beyond traditional parametric models to provide a highly general and flexible framework. The test statistic is constructed using martingale difference divergence (MDD) after neutralizing the effect of Z on Y via a sieve approximation. The population residual MDD characterizes conditional mean independence under suitable moment conditions. We present a theoretical framework for the test under both a fixed number of basis functions and a growing sieve dimension. We derive the nonstandard and non-pivotal asymptotic null distributions in both regimes. To facilitate practical implementation, we propose a wild bootstrap procedure to approximate these limiting distributions and establish its asymptotic consistency. To establish the fundamental properties required for the test to be widely useful, we conduct a power analysis, demonstrating the test's consistency under fixed alternatives and establishing its asymptotic power against local alternatives. The practical utility and finite-sample performance of the proposed test are examined through simulation studies and an exploratory application to a real-world variable selection problem in regression modeling. The code for the proposed test and numerical simulations can be found at: https://github.com/leece087/Conditional-Mean-Independence-Test.

title: Bayesian modeling of predictive stability under generalized Arrhenius non-linear kinetics
comment: 28 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Predictive stability modeling is widely used in pharmaceutical development to establish product shelf-life by identifying the kinetic parameters that govern degradation behavior and using these parameters to extrapolate out in time. Recent approaches typically assume linear degradation dynamics and rely on the Arrhenius equation to model temperature-specific reaction rates. However, observed degradation profiles may reflect nonlinear reaction dynamics and more complex temperature-specific reaction rates, potentially leading to reduced accuracy in long-term predictions and motivating a more flexible approach. We propose a novel Bayesian framework which extends predictive stability modeling beyond simple Arrhenius low-order kinetic dynamics and accommodates complex degradation mechanisms. The degradation process is modeled through the Sestak-Berggren kinetic formulation, a flexible ordinary differential equation encompassing many classical degradation models as special cases. To facilitate model interpretability and model exploration, probabilistic model selection on kinetic parameters automatically determines whether nonlinear reaction components are supported by the data, allowing the model to adaptively collapse to simpler dynamics when appropriate. To address departure from classical Arrhenius kinetics, we develop a generalized temperature reaction rate formulation in which temperature-specific reaction rates are shrunk toward Arrhenius predictions through a hierarchical shrinkage prior while allowing departures when supported by the data. This approach yields robustness to misspecification and reduces sensitivity to potentially influential high-temperature observations commonly encountered in accelerated stability experiments. The resulting framework provides a principled and flexible statistical tool for model-informed shelf-life determination.

title: Null-Corrected Conditional Coverage in Materials Property Prediction: A Five-Dataset Replication
comment: N pages, 15 tables. Extends and partly revises arXiv:2608.07589. Submitted to Data-Centric Engineering. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22213087
summary: Uncertainty quantification for materials property prediction increasingly reports conditional coverage, coverage within strata of the predicted value, alongside marginal coverage. The worst-bin statistics used for this are downward-biased in finite samples, a known defect that applied materials work does not generally correct for. We replicate a single-dataset conditional coverage study across five regression datasets (n = 437 to 21,263), seven interval methods and 50 random splits each, correcting the worst-bin statistic against its expected value under exact conditional validity. The null is simulated from realized per-bin test counts and referenced to each method's own marginal coverage, separating marginal miscalibration from uneven coverage. On the smallest dataset the correction runs from 0.061 to 0.096, between a third and two thirds of the shortfalls actually reported, against 0.009 to 0.011 on the two largest. Split conformal prediction's failure survives the correction on four of five datasets; two conclusions of the antecedent study do not. Conformalized quantile regression, characterized there as a negative case, fails on one dataset only. Cross-fitted normalized conformal prediction, grouped there with the successful methods, fails on three of five. Group-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction stays below our significance criterion on every dataset, yet exceeds the null on three of five under an octile refinement of the variable it calibrates on. A level-matched ablation locates that uniformity in group-conditional calibration rather than in the elevated quantile level, and removes Mondrian's apparent width cost entirely. Conditional coverage evaluations should report the null distribution of the worst-bin statistic used, the method's realized marginal coverage, and the resolution of the evaluation partition relative to any partition the method calibrates on.

title: On Ignorability Beyond Missing at Random: Completion-Invariant Missingness for Nonmonotone Missing Data
summary: The missing-at-random assumption underlies most analyses of incomplete data. Under nonmonotone missingness, it is especially stringent, imposing pattern-specific restrictions with different conditioning sets. A strictly weaker normalization condition is known to justify maximizing the observed-data likelihood. We show that every law satisfying this condition has a unique missing-at-random counterpart sharing its observed-data and complete-data distributions. Observed-data procedures developed under missing at random for identified functionals, including doubly robust estimators, therefore remain valid, with the same semiparametric efficiency bound. We then prove that the condition holds if and only if filling in the missing values from their conditional distribution under the true full model preserves the complete-data distribution, hence the name completion-invariant missingness. We use a characteristic kernel to compare the completed distribution with the fitted model and assess the joint compatibility of the specified full model and completion-invariant missingness. We derive the asymptotic null distribution with estimated parameters and establish bootstrap and multiplier calibration. Since a parametric full model alone need not identify completion-invariant missingness, we give identification conditions for Gaussian, Student $t$ and finite mixture families. Simulations assess sensitivity to departures from each assumption, and applications to clinical laboratory measurements and childhood growth illustrate the diagnostic.

title: Nested Ensemble Learning with Topological Data Analysis for Graph Classification and Regression
comment: This is the published version of the article. Published in International Journal of Topology, MDPI, DOI: 10.3390/ijt2040017. Link to the official version: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijt2040017
summary: We propose a nested ensemble learning framework that utilizes Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to extract and integrate topological features from graph data, with the goal of improving performance on classification and regression tasks. Our approach computes persistence diagrams (PDs) using lower-star filtrations induced by three filter functions: closeness, betweenness, and degree2 centrality. To overcome the limitation of relying on a single filter, these PDs are integrated through a data-driven, three-level architecture. At Level-0, diverse base models are independently trained on the topological features extracted for each filter function. At Level-1, a meta-learner combines the predictions of these base models for each filter to form filter-specific ensembles. Finally, at Level-2, a meta-learner integrates the outputs of these filter-specific ensembles to produce the final prediction. We evaluate our method on both simulated and real-world graph datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms base models and standard stacking methods, achieving higher classification accuracy and lower regression error. It also surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, ranking among the top three models across all benchmarks.

title: One-Sided Randomization in Two-Sided Platform Experiments: Which Side Should be Randomized?
summary:
Two-sided marketplace platforms often use randomized experiments to evaluate new features, raising the question of whether to randomize customers or listings. Randomizing the smaller (\emph{short}) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (\emph{long}) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect.
  Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on {\em both} dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.

title: Regularized trimmed Factorial and Reduced K-means for contaminated high-dimensional data: separating geometry, search and selection
summary: Factorial and Reduced K-means estimate a partition and a low-dimensional clustering subspace jointly, which makes them attractive when the variables that separate groups are not those that dominate total variance. On contaminated high-dimensional data they face three linked problems: trimming can make the scatter matrices singular, the criterion has many local optima, and the rank, number of groups and trimming proportion are unknown and interact. We propose REG-HD-TFKM and REG-HD-TRKM, regularized trimmed versions of the two methods, together with a selection procedure that handles these problems as separate decisions. A ridge-stabilized spectral step keeps every fit well defined; heterogeneous multistart search explores alternative solutions; method-specific agreement and reproducibility scores choose among them; and trimming is applied only when a radial diagnostic or the path over trimming levels supports it. A simulation study with 41 design cells shows why the separation matters. Two representations of euro-area bank balance sheets show that similar partitions can rest on nearly orthogonal subspaces, and that the same selected structure can describe different retained samples.

title: Localizing Mean Shifts in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressive Models
summary:
We study the localization of mean changes in high-dimensional vector autoregressions (VARs) when the autoregressive dynamics remain common across regimes. We develop a three-step procedure that first obtains preliminary change-point estimates from the raw series ignoring the dependence structure, then estimates a common sparse VAR using observations away from the estimated changes, and finally filters the series to refine the change point locations.
  For a single change point, we show that the preliminary localization rate depends directly on the strength of temporal dependence, whereas filtering removes this dependence penalty from the oracle rate. With an estimated filter, the refined rate additionally reflects the error in estimating the VAR dynamics and the relation between the change in the stationary mean and the corresponding change in the VAR intercept. We characterize these rates explicitly and establish conditions under which filtering improves localization. Because filtering near a change point uses lags from adjacent regimes, it also creates a short-lived distortion in the filtered mean; we characterize when this boundary effect is innocuous and develop a transition-corrected alternative.
  We extend the procedure to an unknown number of change points. Overlapping local windows are used to generate candidate locations, an information criterion removes redundant and spurious candidates and estimates the number of changes, and the retained locations are subsequently refined using the estimated VAR filter. We establish consistency for the estimated number of changes and simultaneous localization rates for their locations. Numerical experiments corroborate the localization gains and show robustness to moderate departures from common VAR dynamics. An application to a large panel of U.S. macroeconomic indicators identifies economically interpretable changes.

title: Functional Regression with Interacting Latent Mean and Variance Processes
summary: In many applications, variability itself carries important predictive information beyond the mean, and its association with an outcome may further depend on the underlying mean trajectory. However, existing functional regression approaches primarily rely on mean-based representations of functional predictors, while variability is often ignored or reduced to scalar summaries. We propose a functional regression framework that incorporates latent mean and variance processes as predictors, together with their mean-variance interaction, allowing the predictive contribution of variability to depend on the underlying mean trajectory. We establish consistency and convergence rates for the estimated coefficient functions and interaction surface, accounting for reconstruction errors, increasing observation frequency, and diverging truncation dimensions without requiring independence between the latent processes. Applications to real data demonstrate substantial gains in predictive accuracy from incorporating the variance process, with the proposed approach outperforming competing functional regression methods in the Tecator application and revealing localized mean-variance interaction patterns.

title: Inverse Confounding Analysis: Part 2. Applications to Real- World Observational Data
summary: Unmeasured confounding factors in observational data may lead to biased estimates of the effect of an exposure on an outcome. Consequently, a central problem in causal inference based on observational data is sensitivity analysis with respect to unmeasured confounding. Existing sensitivity-analysis methods generally focus on worst-case bounds. We propose an exact method for quantifying the significance of confounding, defined here in terms of the complete range of analytical values of the stratification-based Risk Ratio over the set of all joint distributions compatible with the observed characteristics. We refer to the proposed method as Inverse Confounding Analysis (ICA) - it is described in [1]. This paper presents examples of applying ICA to several real-world statistical datasets and examines an important issue that has attracted criticism of the method: the practical feasibility of obtaining the input data required for its application. The results are compared with those of two other methods for confounding analysis, the E-value and the method proposed by Pena.

title: Flexible nonlinear spatial autoregressive models under spatial confounding: a gradient boosting approach with closed-form estimation
summary: This paper develops a boosting-based framework for estimating nonlinear spatial autoregressive models (SAR and SEM). Functional gradient descent boosting with spline base learners provides automatic selection of covariates and functional forms, while the spatial parameter is estimated by an extension of the closed-form, determinant-free estimator (CFE) of Smirnov (2020): we show that it remains consistent, with the same asymptotic variance formula, for any additive estimator admitting a smoothing-matrix representation, and we prove that the underlying quasi-score is Neyman-orthogonal to the nonlinear nuisance, which makes the flexible, regularized first stage safe. This flexibility, however, exposes the estimator to a spatial confounding problem that must be solved for the framework to deliver structural estimates. The geoadditive smooth of the coordinates, s(u, v), a default ingredient of flexible spatial specifications, competes with the autoregressive term for the same low-frequency spatial variation, and purely predictive tuning resolves the competition in favour of the surface, biasing the spatial parameter -the geoadditive trap. We therefore equip the estimator with targeted safeguards: a spectral identification diagnostic, a spectral penalty on the surface, spatial cross-fitting, stopping iterations selected by spatial cross-validation, and heteroskedasticity-and spatial-correlation-robust sandwich variances. Monte Carlo experiments, including a factorial design that generates the trap, show that the safeguarded estimators restore test size and confidence-interval coverage while matching maximum likelihood accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost. An empirical application to the Lucas County, Ohio, housing market illustrates the workflow.

title: A Class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions on $SE_n(3)$ for Motion Estimation
summary: This paper proposes a novel class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions (BCDs) on extended special Euclidean groups SE_n(3) for global motion uncertainty representation and estimation. BCDs are constructed by restricting matrix Gaussian distributions on ambient Euclidean space to SE_n(3), avoiding singularity of local coordinates. The unique feature of BCDs is their conjugacy to a broad class of sampling distributions arising in motion estimation, enabling exact closed-form Bayesian inference. Optimal estimation with respect to BCDs is further investigated for implementing motion estimation. Two means are extracted as random state estimates, which maximize probability and minimize mean squared error, respectively. Moreover, within the BCD class, moment matching is shown to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and maximum likelihood estimation is also derived, which provide analytical methods to approximate underlying distributions with the optimality guarantee. As an application, a Bayesian estimator for pose and velocity estimation of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) is developed within an assumed density filtering architecture. The propagation and estimate extraction leverage the optimal estimation related to BCDs, and the landmark measurements are exactly fused with the BCD prior in closed form due to the conjugacy. Numerical simulations of a UAV flight indicate the advantages of BCD-based estimators over two classic Kalman filters on Lie groups with various initial uncertainties and measurement noise.

title: TRACE: Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis
summary: External trial evidence can inform oncology trial design, but broad pooling may produce benchmarks poorly aligned with the planned population. We developed TRACE (Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis), combining eligibility screening, Bayesian compatibility assessment using published baseline characteristics, and hierarchical survival modeling. An integrated compatibility score based on the largest standardized difference in jointly reported characteristics identifies compatible external trials. Their reconstructed control-arm survival data are synthesized using a hierarchical beta-Stacy process to generate a predictive survival benchmark. We evaluated TRACE using eleven randomized phase III trials in first-line HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. With KEYNOTE-859 as the target, three external trials were selected. TRACE predicted a control-arm median overall survival of 11.8 months (95% posterior predictive interval, 8.9-15.2), compared with an observed median of 11.8 months (95% confidence interval, 10.9-12.7). In leave-one-trial-out validation, seven targets had compatible external evidence. Predictive intervals contained the observed median for all seven. In comparison, confidence intervals from Kaplan-Meier estimates pooling all other trials' control arms contained it for five. Mean pointwise curve coverage was 92% for TRACE and 59% for pooled Kaplan-Meier. For four targets without compatible external evidence, TRACE returned a weakly informative prior predictive benchmark. TRACE provides a transparent approach to selecting relevant external evidence and generating benchmarks for oncology trial planning.

title: Identifiability and partial identification under spatial confounding in additive risk models
summary: In spatial risk attribution, continuous environmental exposures and unmeasured background factors often co-vary across broad geographic scales, making it difficult to separate true exposure effects from spatial confounding using finite disease counts. Existing remedies typically project out or penalize shared spatial trends, leaving unclear whether estimation instability stems from the overall capacity of the latent random field or from its directional alignment with exposure. By decomposing the Fisher-weighted smoothing operator of an additive Poisson point process model, we show that while effective degrees of freedom measure total smoothing capacity, the relative loss of Fisher information for the exposure coefficient is governed solely by a distinct directional quantity that we call penalized collinear overlap. Rotating the spatial kernel alters this information loss while holding total capacity fixed, implying that no single smoothing scale is universally optimal. Because real-world confounding combines smooth regional trends with sharp local jumps that escape any moderate basis dictionary, point identification remains fragile. We therefore develop a partial identification framework that bounds residual confounding bias using an observable benchmark covariate. Projecting a joint spatial confidence ellipse yields valid intervals even under weak benchmarks, while incorporating a negative control outcome sharpens the bounds and flags assumption violations. Simulation studies and an analysis of childhood respiratory mortality across England demonstrate the method.

title: GraphInfer: Statistical Inference for Decomposable Graphical Models in R
comment: 44 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. The R package GraphInfer 0.1.0 will be submitted to CRAN; until then, the package and the replication material are available from the author on request
summary: Decomposable graphical models combine closed-form maximum likelihood estimation with local model comparison, which makes structure inference practical with many variables. The R package GraphInfer provides one likelihood framework for decomposable models of continuous, discrete and mixed data, the last as conditional Gaussian models. Structure inference ranges from exact minimum forests and stepwise search to stochastic global search. Nested models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests whose null distributions are exact in finite samples: conditionally on the discrete data for edges with a continuous endpoint, and conditionally on the discrete margins of the smaller model for edges between discrete variables. Missing values are handled by EM, by structural EM, which reuses complete-data searches through a weighted pseudo-sample of expected sufficient statistics, and by multiple imputation; selected models are fit to the observed-data likelihood. The package also treats the graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees: a search over the compatible graphs whose tree moves overcome an obstruction to single-edge moves, fitting of the full accumulation model with measurement noise and bootstrap tests of the accumulation hypothesis. GraphInfer is an independent, pure R successor to the archived package gRapHD. The implementation is validated against independent references, and simulation studies inform its defaults.

title: When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems
summary: In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the type and difficulty of subsequent tasks. Thus model responses can influence the set of prompts on which the model is subsequently evaluated. We study the implications of this user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity for the evaluation of LLMs. We define two classes of estimands for comparing models: the common-distribution effect, which compares model performance on the same distribution of prompts, and the induced-distribution effect, which compares each model on the prompt distribution generated through user interaction. We show that offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing target different quantities, with the standard difference-in-means estimators for the two methods converging to the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. This distinction can affect decision-making: the two comparisons can rank models differently and lead to discrepancies in deployment recommendations. We characterize when such ranking reversals occur and provide a sufficient condition under which the rankings are guaranteed to agree. This result provides a practical heuristic for assessing whether offline evaluation is sufficient to reproduce the decision suggested by a live experiment. Third, we show, in a stylized linear model of interactions, that user adaptivity can increase variance in estimation. Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

title: Unequal-probability distributional balance and the Horvitz-Thompson estimator
summary: Auxiliary information can improve estimation precision under probability sampling, but the relationship between the study and auxiliary variables may not be known well enough to specify suitable balancing variables. Distributionally balanced designs address this by targeting agreement between sample and population auxiliary distributions. We extend energy-based distributional balance to prescribed unequal inclusion probabilities by comparing the empirical sample distribution with an inclusion-probability-weighted population distribution. Under a regularity condition relating the study values divided by their inclusion probabilities to the auxiliaries, we establish an upper bound on the design variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator in terms of the expected energy distance. This bound motivates an algorithm that exchanges units between randomly paired candidate samples without increasing their average energy distance. Combined with random initialization and uniform selection of a final candidate, the procedure preserves the prescribed first-order inclusion probabilities. We evaluate its auxiliary-space properties and estimation performance using generated populations and the Meuse data.

title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: an uncertainty-aware framework, with an application to global cardiovascular disease burden, 1990 to 2023
summary: Modelled health estimates such as those of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study are increasingly used in secondary analyses designed for observed data. However, trajectory clustering typically ignores published uncertainty, selects the number of clusters using criteria blind to it, and assigns countries to groups with unwarranted certainty. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that separates trajectory level from shape, quantifies membership probabilities by perturbing estimates within their uncertainty intervals, selects clusters based on stability under uncertainty, and examines the roles of development, region, and measurement quality. Applied to age-standardised cardiovascular disease DALY rates for 201 countries from 1990-2023 (GBD 2023), the framework identified two stable trajectory types, whereas the gap statistic selected three. The additional cluster was poorly supported (median membership probability 0.70) and disappeared once uncertainty was considered. The retained clusters had similar burdens in 1990 but diverged markedly over time: a stalled-improvement group of 78 countries (median change $-8\%$, 40 of them in sub-Saharan Africa) and a sustained-decline group of 92 countries ($-52\%$). Thirty-one countries remained unclassified because their memberships were uncertain. Results were reproduced using mortality rates, a 2000-2023 analysis window, and bootstrap resampling. Among countries with the narrowest uncertainty intervals, a third well-supported trajectory emerged in former Soviet and Eastern European countries. These findings show that uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters. Ignoring it risks over-interpreting unstable groups and overstating confidence in country classifications. Incorporating published uncertainty and measurement quality should become standard practice when clustering modelled health estimates.

title: Two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems for high-dimensional data: noncentral normal-reference inference
summary: We study noncentral normal-reference inference for high-dimensional two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems. Within the Gaussian reference, a shifted null law is accurate if and only if covariance-weighted signal energy is negligible relative to the trace of the squared covariance. We establish the sharp uniform fourth-root error order over unrestricted spectra and a linear bound under spectral spread. A separate spectral-range criterion determines when signal magnitude alone suffices. An augmented spherical reference gives finite-sample calibration for Gaussian samples and asymptotically recovers Gaussian-reference local power under projection fourth-moment bounds and control of diagonal fluctuations, without a dimension-to-sample-size restriction. For unknown Gaussian covariance, explicit trace and hollow-Gram confidence bounds turn the linear approximation bound into a simultaneous, computable certificate over local effect ranges. Eigenspace signal energies describe directional power, while a two-point argument limits estimation of unknown local power. Simulations with 10,000 evaluation replications per configuration examine unequal and noncommuting covariances, severe sample imbalance, non-Gaussian observations and the informativeness of the certificate.

title: The exact region of the Average Rectangular Volume and Spearman's rho, with an application to arachnitude
summary: The average rectangular volume ($\ARV$) of a bivariate aggregation function is the average of its volumes over all axis-parallel rectangles of the unit square; for a copula, it is the expected copula volume of the rectangle spanned by two independent uniform points. We determine the exact region of the pairs $(\ARV(C),ρ(C))$, where $C$ ranges over all bivariate copulas and $ρ$ is Spearman's rho. The region is compact, convex and symmetric, and its upper boundary consists of three analytically parametrized arcs. A previously proposed family of shuffles of Min generates one arc, but only on part of its range; the other two arcs are generated by singular copulas whose supports contain hyperbolic branches. The boundary is continuously differentiable away from its left endpoint $\ARV=\frac{11}{120}$, where it has a vertical tangent. The proof uses a folding transformation and explicit Kantorovich potentials for a family of optimal transport problems. Finally, we show that the arachnitude, a rank correlation used in actuarial practice, is an affine transformation of $\ARV$, so that the result also describes the joint region of Spearman's rho and arachnitude.

title: Asymptotic Consistency of a Weighted Nadaraya-Watson Estimator Driven by Fractional Brownian Motion at Random Times
summary: Nonparametric regression conventionally assumes equispaced observations, a premise often violated by empirical data with irregular sampling and long-memory noise. This study establishes the asymptotic mean square ($L^2$) consistency of a weighted Nadaraya-Watson (wN-W) estimator for stochastic processes sampled at random times and perturbed by fractional Brownian motion (fBm). Leveraging the occupation time formula and Fernique's Theorem, we derive exact parametric restrictions on bandwidth and sampling rates ensuring convergence. We validate these theoretical findings via extensive simulations evaluating the mean squared error under varying noise persistence. Crucially, we explicitly benchmark the performance of the estimator under random sampling times against classical deterministic grids, while assessing the relative efficiency of quartic versus Gaussian kernels. Finally, we introduce an interactive Shiny application to dynamically visualize the admissible parameter space, and we empirically validate our theoretical framework by applying the estimator to the Vostok ice core paleoclimatological dataset. This real-world application demonstrates the practical capacity of the methodology to extract macroscopic trends while robustly avoiding severe overfitting under random sampling times.\

title: Don't Match the Noise: Distribution Matching under Unknown Measurement Error with an Audit Sample
summary: Real-world machine learning systems often operate on imperfect measurements: sensors are noisy, annotations are produced by non-experts, and scientific observations are often indirect. In these settings, classic distribution comparison tools such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) can be systematically biased, matching artifacts of the measurement process rather than the underlying mechanisms of interest. We study a practical regime in which noisy observations are abundant, but only a small audited subset contains ground-truth measurements. We propose measurement-error-corrected MMD (MEC-MMD), an audit-based estimator that debiases kernel evaluations without requiring a noise model. MEC-MMD is exactly unbiased for the oracle MMD under simple random auditing, admits an explicit variance decomposition, and is consistent for the population MMD, achieving the standard $O_p(N^{-1/2})$ rate when the audit size scales with the dataset. We demonstrate the utility of distributional matching with MEC-MMD loss for both parameter estimation and unsupervised applications, showing that MEC-MMD consistently outperforms MMD and alternative methods. These results provide a principled foundation for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference, and learning in noisy real-world machine learning pipelines.

title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Fairness under Data Imbalance: Theory and Adaptive Allocation
summary: Data imbalance across sensitive groups and class labels is common in classification problems and can contribute to substantial fairness disparities. We study how such imbalance affects Equal Opportunity and how synthetic data augmentation can mitigate the resulting unfairness. We first identify two mechanisms, prevalence imbalance and group-size imbalance, through which changes in the training distribution shift the learned decision boundary and induce disparities in group true positive rates. Motivated by this analysis, we study exact full-balance augmentation, which equalizes all group-label cells. We establish conditions under which full balancing strictly improves Equal Opportunity together with a prediction-error comparison under the oracle balanced distribution, and show that the Equal Opportunity gap of the synthetic-data classifier converges to that of the oracle balanced classifier as the sample size grows and the generator error vanishes. The finite-sample convergence rate agrees, up to logarithmic factors and generator-approximation error, with the information-theoretic lower-bound rate under the corresponding regularity regimes. Since exact balancing need not provide the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice, we further propose Accuracy-Constrained Adaptive Synthetic Augmentation (ACASA), which learns both where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated fairness disparity subject to a constraint on predictive accuracy. We provide a finite-sample guarantee comparing the selected augmentation allocation with the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulation studies and real data application support the theoretical findings and demonstrate that synthetic augmentation can substantially reduce fairness disparities while achieving favorable empirical fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

title: Data augmentation for the generalizability and transportability of fairness in a clinical heart failure algorithm
summary: Synthetic data augmentation has been proposed as a way to artificially supplement clinical datasets to address fairness concerns in downstream classification algorithms. This approach is closely related to upweighting or upsampling methods employed for the problem of class imbalance, which have shown mixed empirical results in practice. Synthetic data augmentation also runs the risk of overfitting to the noise present in subgroups with relatively small sample sizes, raising both generalizability and transportability concerns. We present an empirical evaluation of synthetic data augmentation for fairness in tabular data using simulation studies as well as a real-world application of in-hospital mortality classification for heart failure patients in two distinct data samples. We implement upsampling and upweighting methods as benchmarks for the implicit fairness objective of synthetic data augmentation. Our results suggest that the fairness impacts of data augmentation are sensitive to the design of the downstream algorithm as well as the deployment context and its similarity to the training data. It is crucial that studies making generalizability and transportability claims should provide empirical support for these assertions.

title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

title: Empirical Bayes mirror testing for persistent widening of achievement gaps in U.S. school districts
summary: Unequal recovery from pandemic learning losses raises concerns about widening achievement gaps between economically disadvantaged students and their peers. This study seeks to identify districts whose mathematics gaps widened in every annual interval from 2022 to 2025. The analysis uses estimates from the Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA) for 5,600 U.S. school districts. Identifying such districts requires accounting for correlated errors and differing precision in the estimated annual changes, as well as multiplicity. The true annual gap changes in each district form an effect vector, and persistent widening means that every component is positive. To address this class of multiple testing problems, we propose an empirical Bayes mirror procedure. It uses an estimated distribution of effect vectors to guide ranking and covariance-adjusted mirror observations to calibrate selection. The procedure achieves finite-sample false discovery rate (FDR) control under a Gaussian observation model, without requiring accurate estimation of the posterior null probabilities used for ranking. Simulations demonstrate power gains from incorporating information about the distribution of effect vectors. At a target FDR of 25%, the SEDA analysis identifies eight districts in five states with evidence of widening gaps in every annual interval.

title: Global-Local and Window-Concatenated Functional Random Forests: Early and Late Fusion of Window-Specific Functional Principal Components
summary: Functional random forests built on a single functional principal component decomposition of the whole domain may dilute features confined to short intervals, whose location is rarely known in advance. We propose two random forests based on window-specific functional principal components. The global-local functional random forest (GL-FRF) is a late-fusion method that stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights; it contains the full-curve forest as a feasible solution, and its weights indicate which parts of the domain drive the prediction. The window-concatenated functional random forest (WC-FRF) is an early-fusion method that trains a single tuned forest on the concatenated window-specific scores. On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve, whereas GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across all 32 simulated and real settings, which makes it the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown.

title: AIDA: Analysis of Interval Data in R
summary: AIDA is an R package that provides tools for the analysis of interval-valued data, including construction, visualization, robust estimation, and explainable outlier detection. The package is built around the intData class and is designed to support methodological research and applied workflows involving interval-valued data. AIDA implements methods for symbolic covariance estimation based on the Mallows distance, robust estimation via the Interval Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator, and explainable outlier detection using Shapley values. The package also includes visualization tools to support interpretation of the results and several interval-valued datasets.

title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
summary: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks. For homogeneous linear preferential attachment and Norros--Reittu graphs with Pareto weights, we derive the joint limiting law of the selected rank, retained fraction of the threshold tie, and exponent error. The selector retains of order $n^{2/(α+2)}$ of $n$ vertices, where $α$ is the survival exponent. At this rank, integer spacing and finite-degree departures from a Pareto tail have the same order as sampling fluctuations. The exponent estimate is consistent and retains a shift on the scale used for confidence intervals. For integer degree laws whose tail sums have a first-order inverse-degree expansion, adding the retained tie fraction divided by the threshold to the Hill statistic removes the leading contribution of the tie. Under homogeneous preferential attachment with a fixed known number of edges per new vertex, removing the remaining model-specific term and calibrating for selection gives confidence intervals with asymptotically exact coverage. Observed networks show sensitivity of the fitted exponent and the classification of degree variance to threshold ties. Simulations assess interval coverage and show improved pooled connectivity predictions after correction under both specified graph laws. Changes to the Norros--Reittu weight distribution can reverse the prediction gain.

title: Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
summary: Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.
